In Protocol Buffers the datatype annotation on each field tells the parser how many bytes to skip, which is what makes preservation possible; in Avro the equivalent discipline is that fields are added with defaults and resolved by name. Patching the old code is not the fix because the old code is already deployed and running — that is what makes this the hard direction. Even if you patch it now, the whole point of the property is that it must hold for readers you cannot reach mid-upgrade.

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 2 — the nightly relational dump
questions.prompt: A team dumps a relational database to files nightly for analytics. The relational schema changes every few weeks — columns added, occasionally renamed. They currently hand-maintain a Protocol Buffers schema for the dump and an engineer updates the tag mapping each time a column changes. It is error-prone and twice someone has reused a tag. (a) Name the format better suited to this job and the single structural property that makes it so. (b) Explain how a reader copes when the export's field set changes, and what it matches on. (c) Name the new obligation this format creates that Protocol Buffers does not, and give the mechanism appropriate to this use case.
questions.ideal: (a) Avro, and the structural property is that its schema contains no tag numbers — fields are identified by name. That is precisely why it is friendlier to dynamically generated schemas: you can generate an Avro schema from the relational schema on every run, one record per table and one field per column, and the export process need pay no attention to the schema having changed. (b) The reader resolves the writer's schema against the reader's schema, matching fields by name. A field present in the writer's schema but absent from the reader's is ignored; a field the reader expects but the writer's schema lacks is filled from the default declared in the reader's schema. Field order does not matter. With Protocol Buffers this same job would require an administrator to maintain the column-to-tag mapping by hand and be very careful never to reuse a tag — exactly the failure they have already hit twice. (c) The new obligation is conveying the writer's schema, since Avro-encoded data identifies neither field names nor types and is undecodable without it. For this use case — a large file containing many records all encoded with the same schema — the right mechanism is an Avro object container file, which includes the schema once at the beginning of the file. (Credit for naming the other two mechanisms and rejecting them: a per-record version number plus a schema registry suits a database of individually-written records; connection-time negotiation suits two processes on a network connection.)

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 1 — the social app with six followers
questions.prompt: A social app runs one leader and six asynchronous followers, load-balancing reads randomly. Users report three things: their own new posts sometimes vanish on the next page load; a friend's comment appears, then disappears on refresh, then reappears; and after a failover last month, roughly forty seconds of posts were gone permanently. (a) Name each of the three symptoms precisely. (b) Give the specific fix for each of the first two, and say why the fix for the second does not solve the first. (c) Explain the third and name the single most important decision during failover that limits it.
questions.ideal: (a) Posts vanishing after you create them is a read-after-write (read-your-writes) violation. A comment appearing, disappearing and reappearing is a monotonic reads violation — successive reads are served by replicas with different lag, so the user sees time move backward. The forty seconds lost at failover is discarded unreplicated writes under asynchronous replication. (b) For read-after-write: read anything the user may have modified from the leader — for a social app the simple rule is own profile and own posts from the leader, everyone else's from a follower. If too much is user-editable, read from the leader for a period after each write, or have the client remember the timestamp of its last write and serve it only replicas that have caught up past it. For monotonic reads: make each user always read from the same replica, chosen deterministically, for example by a hash of the user ID rather than at random. Pinning does not solve read-after-write, because the replica a user is pinned to can still lag behind their own most recent write — consistency of which replica is not the same as freshness of that replica. (c) At failover a follower is promoted; with asynchronous replication it may not have received the old leader's most recent writes, and the standard resolution is to discard them — so writes confirmed to clients turn out not to have been durable. The decision that limits the damage is choosing the most up-to-date follower: with semisynchronous replication, the follower the leader waited on; with asynchronous, the one with the highest log sequence number. Losing a fraction of a second may be tolerable; promoting a replica days behind would be catastrophic. Credit for naming the GitHub incident's shape — a lagging promoted leader reusing autoincrement primary keys, causing inconsistency with an external store and disclosing private data to the wrong users.

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 2 — three regional leaders and two constraints
questions.prompt: A team wants users in three regions to get fast writes, so they propose a leader in each region replicating asynchronously to the others. The product requires that usernames be globally unique and that a prepaid balance can never go negative. An architect suggests "we'll just add a uniqueness constraint and a check constraint". (a) Name the architecture and explain, mechanically, why both constraints are unenforceable under it. (b) Say whether this is a limitation of the database product, and justify the answer. (c) Give the two structural options, name one topology hazard they should know about regardless, and say which option you'd take.
questions.ideal: (a) It is multi-leader replication with asynchronous replication between regions. Neither constraint is enforceable because each leader validates against only its own local state at the time of the write. Two users can register the same username in two regions simultaneously: each write passes the uniqueness check locally, both succeed, and the conflict only surfaces when the writes replicate — after both clients have been told they succeeded. The balance case is the same shape: two withdrawals in different regions can each leave a non-negative balance individually while together taking the account below zero. The constraint spans writes that were never evaluated together. (b) No — this is not a product limitation. It is a fundamental limitation of distributed systems: if two nodes can accept writes without coordinating, no amount of engineering in the database will let them enforce a constraint that depends on both writes being seen together. Switching vendors will not help. Credit for noting that multi-leader is often a retrofitted feature, so autoincrementing keys, triggers and integrity constraints also interact badly — but that is a separate, weaker point. (c) Two structural options. Either use a single leader for the data carrying these constraints, accepting cross-region write latency for those operations — possibly while keeping other data multi-leader. Or drop the constraints as hard guarantees and handle violations after the fact: detect duplicate usernames and force a rename, allow the balance to go negative and reconcile. The topology hazard to know regardless: in an all-to-all topology, replication messages can overtake one another, so a replica may receive an update to a row before the insert that created it — a causality problem that timestamps cannot fix and that needs version vectors. I would take the single-leader option for the constrained data: the constraints are stated as product requirements, and the honest cost is latency on those specific writes rather than a class of bug that surfaces as duplicate accounts and negative balances.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 1 — pings keyed by timestamp
questions.prompt: A fleet-tracking system stores position pings keyed by timestamp, sharded by key range across twelve nodes. The main query is "all pings in the last hour". One node runs at 95% CPU while the other eleven idle. An engineer proposes switching to hash sharding on the timestamp. (a) Explain the current hot shard mechanically, and say whether the scheme or the key is at fault. (b) State exactly what the proposed fix would break, and why that matters given their main query. (c) Give the better fix, and name the query cost it imposes.
questions.ideal: (a) With key-range sharding on a timestamp, shards correspond to contiguous ranges of time. All current writes therefore land in the shard owning the present range, while every other shard holds only historical data and takes no write traffic. The key is at fault, not the scheme: key-range sharding is behaving exactly as designed, and it is the monotonically increasing partition key that concentrates the writes. (b) Hashing the timestamp would spread the writes evenly, but it would destroy range scans over the partition key, because keys that are adjacent in time would be scattered across every shard. Their main query is "all pings in the last hour" — precisely a range scan over the partition key — so the proposed fix would turn their single most important query into a scatter-gather across all twelve nodes. It trades a hot shard for a slow system. (c) Make the partition key compound, with something spreading first and the timestamp second — vehicle ID then timestamp. Writes then distribute across shards by vehicle while remaining sorted by time within each vehicle. The cost is that a query spanning all vehicles for a time range now needs a separate range query per vehicle, whose results must be combined. Credit for noting the general principle: keep the partition key's first component spreading and range-scan the later components, so scans stay within a shard.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 2 — the institutional buyer and the self-healing cluster
questions.prompt: A marketplace shards orders by buyer_id using a fixed 256-shard scheme over 16 nodes. A single institutional buyer now generates 40% of all writes. Someone suggests raising the shard count to 4,096 to spread the load. Separately, the cluster recently "healed itself" during a traffic spike and the outage got worse for twenty minutes. (a) Explain why raising the shard count will not help, using the right term for the problem. (b) Give the two available responses, and state precisely what the application-level one does and does not reduce. (c) Explain the self-healing incident, and say what you would change about the rebalancing policy.
questions.ideal: (a) Because this is a hot key, not a hot shard. All that buyer's orders share one buyer_id, so they hash to one value and land in one shard no matter how many shards exist. Raising the count from 256 to 4,096 subdivides everything except the thing causing the problem — and it costs an expensive resharding, since every shard must be split and rewritten. Consistent hashing distributes keys uniformly, which is not the same as distributing load uniformly. (b) Either isolate the hot key — a range-based scheme can put an individual hot key in a shard by itself, potentially on a dedicated machine — or split it at the application level by appending a random suffix, so two digits spread the writes across 100 keys. Be precise about what the second buys: it splits the write load only. Reads must now query all 100 keys and combine the results, so the read volume against that data is unchanged. It also needs bookkeeping to record which keys are split, and a process for promoting a normal key to a split one, since applying it to every key would be pure overhead. (c) The incident is automatic rebalancing interacting with automatic failure detection. A node was overloaded by the spike and became slow; its peers concluded it was dead and rebalanced its shards away; moving that data added load to the network and the remaining nodes, making them slow, and risking further false suspicions — a cascading failure caused entirely by the automation. I would put a human in the loop for rebalancing, accepting that it is slower in exchange for avoiding operational surprises, and rebalance pre-emptively ahead of known traffic events rather than reactively during them.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 1 — the paused worker and the corrupted file
questions.prompt: A job scheduler uses a lock service so that exactly one worker processes each input file. A worker acquires the lock, begins writing output, suffers a two-minute garbage collection pause, and resumes. Meanwhile the lease expired, a second worker acquired it and wrote its own output. The file is now corrupt. The team proposes reducing GC pauses and doubling the lease duration. (a) Name what the first worker became and explain why the proposed fix cannot eliminate the problem. (b) Name the mechanism that does solve it, describe precisely how it rejects the stale write, and say what a client should do immediately on acquiring a lease. (c) Name the popular alternative approach and give two reasons it is ineffective.
questions.ideal: (a) The first worker became a zombie — a former leaseholder that has not yet discovered it lost the lease and continues acting as though it still holds it, with no awareness that time has passed. The proposed fix cannot eliminate the problem because it only makes the window smaller, never zero: garbage collection pauses can be reduced but not abolished, and the same failure arises with no pause at all if a write request is merely delayed in the network and arrives after the lease has been reassigned — packets can be delayed by a minute or more. Any fix based on making the timing better is fighting an unbounded quantity. (b) Fencing tokens. The lock service returns a number with every grant that increases each time a lease is issued. Every write to the storage service must carry the client's current token, and the storage service remembers the highest token it has processed and rejects any write carrying a lower one. So worker 1 holds token 33, pauses, and worker 2 acquires 34 and writes; when worker 1 wakes and writes with 33, the service rejects it because it has already accepted 34. On acquiring a lease a client should immediately make a write, because once that write completes any earlier zombie is fenced off. Credit for noting that a conditional-write or compare-and-set facility — S3's conditional writes, Azure's conditional headers, Google Cloud Storage's request preconditions — achieves the same effect for a single storage service. (c) The popular alternative is shutting the zombie down — disconnecting it from the network, stopping the VM, or powering the machine off, sometimes called STONITH. It is ineffective for two reasons: it does not protect against a delayed write already in flight from a client that has since crashed, and by the time the zombie is detected and shut down the damage may already be done. A third acceptable answer: badly designed shutdown mechanisms can result in all the nodes shutting one another down.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 2 — writes that never take effect
questions.prompt: A multi-region key-value store resolves conflicts by last-write-wins on the client's time-of-day timestamp. An engineer reports that a small number of updates "never take effect" — the write returns success, and a later read shows the old value. It correlates loosely with one region. Clocks are NTP-synchronised and skew is measured at under 5 ms. (a) Explain the mechanism, and why sub-5 ms skew does not make it safe. (b) Name the second, distinct defect of last-write-wins that this system also has, and the mechanism that addresses it. (c) Say why this class of fault is especially dangerous operationally, compared with a node that crashes.
questions.ideal: (a) Under last-write-wins the replica keeps whichever value carries the greatest timestamp and discards the rest. A node whose clock lags is therefore unable to overwrite a value previously written by a node with a faster clock until the skew between them has elapsed. The write is accepted and acknowledged, then silently discarded during conflict resolution — no error is reported to the application, which is why it looks like the write "never took effect". Sub-5 ms skew does not make this safe because safety here is not a function of how small the skew is: the worked example loses an increment with skew under 3 ms, since what matters is whether the causally-later write happens to receive a smaller timestamp, and any positive skew makes that possible. Correlating with one region is the expected fingerprint of one group of clocks running slightly slow. (b) The second defect is that last-write-wins cannot distinguish genuinely concurrent writes from sequential ones — writes that occurred in quick succession, where the second causally depends on the first, are treated identically to writes where neither writer knew about the other. The mechanism that addresses it is version vectors, which track causality explicitly rather than inferring it from time. (A third defect worth credit: two nodes can generate the same timestamp at millisecond resolution, needing a tiebreaker that can itself violate causality.) (c) Because clock faults fail silently. A defective CPU or a misconfigured network breaks loudly and gets fixed quickly; a drifting quartz clock or a misconfigured NTP client lets everything appear to work while diverging further from reality, so the result is silent, subtle data loss rather than a dramatic crash. Nobody is paged, nothing appears in a dashboard, and the loss is discovered — if ever — long afterwards by a user. The operational implication is that you must monitor clock offsets across the cluster and evict any node whose clock drifts too far, because the system will not tell you.

questions.prompt: Define backward and forward compatibility without using either word, and say which one a rolling upgrade forces on you and why it cannot be fixed by deploying a patch.
questions.ideal: Backward compatibility: newer code can read data written by older code. Forward compatibility: older code can read data written by newer code. A rolling upgrade forces forward compatibility on you, because during the upgrade some instances are already running the new version and writing new data while others are still running the old version and reading it. It cannot be fixed by deploying a patch because the readers that must cope are the ones already deployed and running — that is the whole difficulty: backward compatibility is easy since you know the old format when you write the new code, while forward compatibility requires old code to tolerate a format nobody had written yet when that code shipped.

questions.prompt: An old instance reads a record containing a field it has never heard of, then writes the record back. What must the encoding guarantee, and what is lost if it doesn't?
questions.ideal: The encoding must let the old reader skip a field it does not recognise and preserve it when it writes the record back — not merely ignore it. In Protocol Buffers the datatype annotation on each field tells the parser how many bytes to skip, which is what makes preservation possible; in Avro the discipline is that fields are added with defaults and resolved by name. If the encoding does not guarantee it, the old instance drops the unrecognised field from its in-memory representation and writes the record back without it, so the data is silently lost. The fingerprint is that only records which were modified lose the field — records created and never touched again keep it.

questions.prompt: Name the three replication log implementations, and give the specific defect of each that the others avoid.
questions.ideal: Statement-based: ship the SQL statement itself. Its defect is nondeterminism — NOW(), RAND(), autoincrements and triggers make the follower diverge subtly from the leader. WAL shipping: ship the storage engine's write-ahead log. Its defect is that the log describes data at a very low level and is tightly coupled to the storage engine, so leader and follower usually cannot run different versions, which forbids zero-downtime upgrades. Logical (row-based) log — for example MySQL's binlog: ship row-level change records in a format decoupled from the storage internals. It avoids both defects — it is deterministic and it can stay backward compatible across versions, and because it is parseable by outside systems it is the basis of change data capture. Its cost is that the database must produce a second log on top of the write-ahead log it already keeps for durability — MySQL maintains a separate binlog alongside the WAL, while PostgreSQL derives its logical log by decoding the physical WAL.

questions.prompt: A user posts a comment and it vanishes on reload; another user sees a comment appear, vanish and reappear. Name both anomalies and give the fix for each, then say why one fix doesn't solve the other.
questions.ideal: The vanishing comment is a read-after-write (read-your-writes) violation; the comment that appears, vanishes and reappears is a monotonic reads violation — successive reads are served by replicas with different lag, so the user sees time move backward. Fix for read-after-write: read anything the user may have modified from the leader, or read from the leader for a period after each write, or have the client remember the timestamp of its last write and be served only replicas that have caught up past it. Fix for monotonic reads: always route a given user to the same replica, chosen deterministically — for example by a hash of the user ID rather than at random. Pinning does not solve read-after-write, because the replica a user is pinned to can still lag behind that user's own most recent write: consistency of which replica you read is not the same as freshness of that replica.

questions.prompt: State the quorum condition, work out what n=5, w=3, r=3 tolerates, and give two reasons the condition can hold while a read still returns a stale value.
questions.ideal: The condition is w + r > n: the write set and the read set are then guaranteed to overlap in at least one node, so at least one node you read holds the latest value. With n=5, w=3, r=3 you tolerate two unavailable nodes — writes still find three, reads still find three, and 3 + 3 > 5. Note it need not be a majority; only the overlap matters. Reasons it can hold and still return a stale value (any two): a sloppy quorum, where writes were accepted on any reachable replica rather than the usual ones, so the overlap guarantee no longer applies; a read concurrent with a write, where it is undefined which value is returned; a write that partially succeeded, having been written to fewer than w nodes without being rolled back on those that took it; a node that failed and was restored from an old backup, breaking the count of replicas holding the new value; and rebalancing. Treat w and r as tuning the probability of staleness, not as an absolute guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why can a multi-leader system not guarantee unique usernames? Is this the database's fault?
questions.ideal: Because each leader validates the write against only its own local state at the time of the write. Two users can register the same username in two regions simultaneously: both checks pass locally, both writes are confirmed to their clients, and the conflict surfaces only when the writes replicate asynchronously — after the fact. No, it is not the database's fault. It is a fundamental limitation of distributed systems: if two nodes can accept writes without coordinating, no engineering in the database can enforce a constraint that depends on both writes being evaluated together, and switching vendors will not help. The structural options are to route the constrained data through a single leader, accepting cross-region write latency for those operations, or to drop the constraint as a hard guarantee and reconcile violations afterwards.

questions.prompt: A table sharded by timestamp has one saturated node. Explain the mechanism, say whether the key or the scheme is at fault, and give the fix along with the query cost it imposes.
questions.ideal: The mechanism: with key-range sharding, shards own contiguous ranges of the key, so if the key is a timestamp all current writes land in the one shard that owns the present range while every other shard holds only historical data and takes no write traffic. The key is at fault, not the scheme — key-range sharding is behaving exactly as designed, and it is the monotonically increasing partition key that concentrates the writes. The fix is to make the partition key compound, with something spreading first and the timestamp second — for example vehicle ID then timestamp — so writes distribute across shards while staying sorted by time within each. The query cost: a query spanning all vehicles for a time range now needs a separate range query per prefix value, whose results must be combined.

questions.prompt: Explain why hashing fixes a hot shard but not a hot key, and state precisely what the random-suffix workaround does and does not reduce.
questions.ideal: Hashing fixes a hot shard because a hot shard is an artefact of the layout — an uneven distribution of distinct keys across ranges — and a hash function spreads distinct keys evenly. It cannot fix a hot key because all the traffic shares one key, which hashes to one value and therefore lands on one shard no matter how many shards exist; the unevenness is in the traffic, not the layout. Raising the shard count subdivides everything except the thing causing the problem. The random-suffix workaround — appending, say, two random digits so the writes spread across 100 keys — reduces the write load on any single key. It does not reduce the read volume: reads must now query all 100 keys and combine the results, so the read work against that data goes up rather than down. It also requires bookkeeping to record which keys are split and a process for promoting a normal key to a split one, since applying it everywhere is pure overhead.

questions.prompt: You send a request and receive no reply. List at least four distinct things that may have happened, and say what a longer timeout would tell you about which one it was.
questions.ideal: At least four of: the request was lost before it arrived; the request is sitting in a queue and will be delivered later; the remote node failed — crashed or was powered down; the remote node is paused, for example in a long garbage collection, and will resume later; the node processed the request and the response was lost on the way back; the node processed it and the response is merely delayed. A longer timeout tells you nothing about which one it was. A timeout is a decision to stop waiting and act on a guess, not a discovery: because delay is unbounded, no amount of extra waiting converts the guess into knowledge — it only trades users waiting through an outage against the risk of declaring a live node dead.

questions.prompt: A client pauses for two minutes, its lease expires, another client takes over, and the first wakes up and writes. Name what it has become, why you cannot prevent it, and the mechanism that makes its write harmless.
questions.ideal: The first client has become a zombie — a former leaseholder that has not discovered it lost the lease and carries on as though it still holds it, with no awareness that time has passed. You cannot prevent it because the window can be made smaller but never zero: process pauses can be reduced but not abolished, and the identical failure occurs with no pause at all if a write is merely delayed in the network and arrives after the lease has been reassigned. The mechanism that makes the write harmless is the fencing token: the lock service returns a number that increases with every grant, every write must carry it, and the storage service remembers the highest token it has accepted and rejects any write carrying a lower one. So the woken client's write with the old token is rejected. A client should make a write immediately on acquiring a lease, because once that write lands any earlier zombie is fenced off.

competencies.title: Transactions — Isolation Levels, Serializability, Atomic Commit
parts: The weak levels, and what they stop
What they don't stop, and the three roads back

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 1 — the store that is "atomic, so we're covered"
questions.prompt: A team stores each order as a single document and also maintains a separate order_totals summary row per customer, plus a secondary index on order status. They have no multi-object transactions — the store offers atomic single-document updates and a conditional write, which they describe as "atomic, so we're covered". Support reports two recurring issues: totals that don't match the sum of a customer's orders, and orders that appear when filtering by status but not when listed directly. (a) Name the two guarantees they believe they have and say precisely what each one does and does not cover. (b) Explain the mechanism behind each of the two reported symptoms. (c) The team proposes retrying any failed write until it succeeds. Give two distinct reasons this does not fix the problem, one of which must not depend on the network.
questions.ideal: (a) They have single-object atomicity and isolation — no reader sees a half-written document, a crash doesn't splice old and new values, an interrupted write doesn't persist a fragment — and an atomic conditional write, which prevents lost updates on one object by applying the change only if the value hasn't moved since they read it. Both are genuine and both are scoped to one object. Neither says anything about two objects changing together, which is precisely what they need. A store offering linearizable reads and conditional writes on single objects has not given anyone transactions. (b) The mismatched totals are a multi-object atomicity failure: the order document and the summary row are separate objects, so a fault after one write and before the other leaves them permanently disagreeing, and without atomicity nobody can tell which writes took effect. The index symptom is the same fault in a place people forget: a secondary index is a separate database object, so without isolation a record can appear in one index and not another because the second index update hasn't happened yet. Credit for noting that this makes almost every write multi-object whether the team intended it or not. (c) First reason, not depending on the network: retrying does not undo the write that already succeeded. Without atomicity there is nothing to roll back, so a retry of the pair re-applies the half that worked and can double-count the summary — this is the "best effort, won't undo what it has done" posture, and error recovery is now the application's problem. Second reason: the write may have succeeded with the acknowledgment lost, so the retry performs it twice unless they add application-level deduplication. Also creditable: retrying is pointless after a permanent error such as a constraint violation, and retrying under contention makes an overload worse.

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 2 — two unsafe statements about ACID
questions.prompt: A payments service runs on a database advertised as ACID compliant. During an incident review, an engineer says: "the database guarantees consistency, so a negative balance is impossible". A second engineer says: "and it's durable, so once we return 200 to the client the money has definitely moved". Neither statement is safe as stated. (a) Correct the first statement, naming what the database will and will not enforce and what the team must do about it. (b) Correct the second, giving two distinct ways a committed write can still be lost. (c) The service sends a confirmation email inside the transaction and retries the whole transaction on any error. Name the specific hazard and say what has to change.
questions.ideal: (a) The database enforces the invariants that were declared as constraints — a check constraint on the balance column would genuinely prevent a negative value. It cannot enforce an invariant nobody declared, and it cannot express many complex invariants at all, particularly those spanning multiple rows. The C in ACID therefore depends on how the application uses the database and is not a property of the database alone: if the rule matters, declare it, and where it can't be declared, the application must define its transactions so they preserve it. (Extra credit for noting that the word has at least five meanings and that "ACID compliant" tells you almost nothing about which isolation level you have.) (b) Two of: a correlated fault — a power outage, or a bug that crashes every node on the same input — losing anything held only in memory across all replicas at once; asynchronous replication discarding recent writes when the leader becomes unavailable; a storage-level failure, since drives can violate their guarantees on sudden power loss, firmware has bugs, disk data can silently corrode, and fsync is genuinely hard to use correctly. Not creditable: the machine dying with the disk intact — that data is inaccessible until you fix the machine or move the disk, which is a different failure from losing it. The general point: there is no perfect durability, only risk-reduction techniques — disk, replication, backups — that should be used together. (c) The hazard is a side effect outside the database. Aborting the transaction rolls back the writes but does not unsend the email, so every retry sends another. The fix is to move the send out of the transaction and make it idempotent — record the intent inside the transaction, send afterwards keyed on something unique so a repeat send can be suppressed. Credit for noting the general rule: retry only after transient errors, bound the retries with exponential backoff, and remember that a retry can also duplicate the work if the commit succeeded and the acknowledgment was lost.

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 1 — the four-hour export that doesn't balance
questions.prompt: A nightly job exports the whole database to a file for regulatory reporting. It runs at read-committed isolation and takes about four hours. Auditors report that the exported ledger does not balance: a handful of transfers appear to have a debit with no matching credit, or the reverse. The team's proposed fix is to run the export at 3 a.m. "when almost nothing is happening", and to re-run it if the totals don't match. (a) Name the anomaly and explain why no value in the export was ever wrong. (b) Say why both parts of the proposed fix are the wrong shape of solution. (c) Name the isolation level that solves it, describe the mechanism that implements it, and state the operational cost the team should watch for once they switch.
questions.ideal: (a) Read skew, also called a nonrepeatable read. Under read committed each read returns a value that was committed at the instant it was read — so no individual value in the export was ever wrong. The problem is that the export reads different parts of the database at different moments, and a transfer that lands between two of those moments is seen from one side only: the debit is captured after it happened and the matching credit before it did, or the reverse. The set of values was never simultaneously true, even though every element of it was. (b) Running at 3 a.m. treats the problem as a probability, but the exposure window is the whole four hours of the export, not a busy period — a single transfer anywhere in it produces the defect, and quiet hours only make it rarer and therefore harder to catch. Re-running on mismatch is worse: it is a detection mechanism dressed as a fix, and it only works for imbalances that happen to be detectable by totals. A skewed export whose figures happen to balance is still wrong, and this class of error becomes permanent the moment anyone restores or reports from it. (c) Snapshot isolation. The mechanism is multiversion concurrency control: every transaction gets an always-increasing id, every written row is tagged with the id of the writer, an update is internally a delete plus an insert, and visibility rules hide writes from transactions that were in progress when the reader started, writes from later ids, and writes from aborted transactions. So the export reads the database exactly as it stood when it began, while writes continue unblocked — readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The operational cost to watch: the database must retain every row version the long-running export might still need, so garbage collection stalls and storage grows for as long as the snapshot is open. Monitor the age of the oldest open transaction.

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 2 — the reconciliation query that shouldn't block anything
questions.prompt: Two services share a database. Service A runs short write transactions. Service B runs a five-minute read-only reconciliation query every hour. After a migration, Service A's p99 latency becomes spiky, and every spike lines up with Service B's query. Separately, the storage team reports the table's on-disk size growing steadily even though row counts are flat, and a colleague suggests that this proves the snapshot mechanism is leaking. (a) Under a correct MVCC implementation, what should the relationship between B's reads and A's writes be, and what does the observed blocking tell you about how the database is configured? (b) Explain the disk growth without assuming a bug, and name the specific thing to look for. (c) The team wants B to keep its coherent view but stop affecting A. Say what you would change and what you would monitor.
questions.ideal: (a) Under MVCC the relationship should be no relationship at all: reads take no locks, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers — that is the defining performance property of snapshot isolation. Observed blocking therefore says the reads are taking locks, which means the database is not serving B from a snapshot: either the read-committed implementation in use prevents dirty reads with read locks rather than by keeping the old committed value, or B is running under two-phase locking, where a large scan takes a shared lock over everything it reads and writers must wait for it. (b) It is the expected consequence of never updating in place. Under MVCC an update is a delete plus an insert, so modified rows accumulate versions; a version can only be garbage-collected once no open transaction could still need it. B's five-minute snapshot pins every version that existed when it started, so five minutes of write traffic is retained on every run, and any transaction left open longer pins proportionally more. Flat row counts with growing size is the signature, not a contradiction. Look for the oldest open transaction — that one number explains the retention. Note that the two symptoms only coexist under one reading: an MVCC engine, with B's scan taking locks because it is running under two-phase locking. An engine that prevented dirty reads with read locks instead of by keeping old committed values would block A's writes but would not accumulate versions, so the disk growth is what tells you which diagnosis in (a) is the live one. (c) Put B on snapshot isolation so its coherent view costs no locks — that is exactly the workload snapshot isolation exists for, alongside backups and integrity checks. If the blocking came from a read-committed implementation using read locks, change that setting rather than weakening B's guarantee. Monitor the age of the oldest open snapshot and the growth of dead row versions, since the cost has moved from latency to storage and garbage-collection lag, and a query that hangs now costs disk instead of blocking writers.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 1 — overselling seats and losing note lines
questions.prompt: A ticketing system holds a fixed pool of seats. To sell a seat, a transaction counts unsold seats in the section, and if the count is above zero, inserts a sale row. Under load, sections occasionally oversell by one or two. An engineer proposes locking the counted rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Separately, the same system has a "seat notes" field that agents edit by reading the whole note, appending a line and writing it back; notes occasionally lose an agent's line. (a) Name both anomalies, say which one is the general case, and explain why. (b) Say whether the proposed FOR UPDATE fix works for the overselling, and justify the answer mechanically. (c) Give the most appropriate fix for the lost note lines and one alternative, and say what each assumes about the data.
questions.ideal: (a) The overselling is write skew; the vanishing note lines are a lost update. Write skew is the general case: two transactions read the same objects and then update different objects, so nothing is overwritten and no single transaction breaks the rule. A lost update is the special case where the different transactions happen to update the same object, so the second write clobbers the first. In the seats example each transaction counts the same rows and then inserts its own sale row; in the notes example both agents read and rewrite the same field. (b) No. The check is a COUNT over unsold seats and the write is an INSERT of a new sale row — the transaction checks for a condition and then creates a row that changes the result of that condition. That is a phantom. SELECT … FOR UPDATE can only attach locks to rows the query returned, and here the decisive rows are the ones that do not exist yet, so there is nothing to lock. (Contrast the on-call doctors, where the row updated in step 3 was one of the rows returned in step 1 — there the lock does work.) The real options are serializable isolation, which is what predicate and index-range locks were invented for; or materialising the conflict as pre-created lockable rows, one per seat, which is ugly and a last resort; or, if the invariant can be expressed as one, a constraint. (c) Best fix for the notes: an atomic write operation if appending can be expressed as one — the database performs the change without a read-modify-write cycle in application code, which is the usual best answer when it fits. It may not fit arbitrary text, so the alternative is a conditional write (compare-and-set) on the previous content or on a version-number column, checking afterwards that the update took effect and retrying if not. What each assumes: the atomic operation assumes the change is expressible as a database-side operation on one object; the conditional write assumes there is a single up-to-date copy of the value to compare against — which is exactly what multi-leader or leaderless replication cannot give you, where you would instead merge conflicting versions and can only prevent lost updates if the operations commute. Also creditable: an explicit lock, or a level that detects lost updates automatically.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 2 — choosing an implementation of serializability
questions.prompt: A team decides to move to serializable isolation. Their workload is: many short read/write transactions on a small hot set of rows, plus a few long analytical reads. They have two candidate databases — one implementing serializability with two-phase locking, one with serializable snapshot isolation — and a third proposal to run everything through single-threaded stored procedures. Their stated goals are "predictable p99 latency" and "no application changes". (a) Predict the specific failure each of the three options will show on this workload. (b) Say which goal is unachievable regardless of choice, and why. (c) Name the property of their workload that most determines the answer, and say what you would measure before committing.
questions.ideal: (a) Two-phase locking: the hot rows are exactly where 2PL hurts — every transaction that might conflict waits for the other, latency becomes unstable and very bad at high percentiles, and deadlocks (much more frequent at this level) throw away completed work and force retries. The long analytical reads make it worse: a transaction reading large parts of a table takes a shared lock over it, so writes to that table stop until the read commits. SSI: no blocking, but a small hot set means high contention, and optimistic concurrency control degrades precisely there — a large share of transactions abort at commit and the retries add load to a system already near capacity. Serial execution: throughput is capped at one CPU core; one slow transaction stalls every other; and the whole workload must be rewritten as stored procedures submitted in advance, since an interactive statement-at-a-time transaction would leave the single thread waiting on the network. (b) "No application changes" is unachievable. Every route to serializability changes what the application must do. Under 2PL and SSI the transaction can be aborted — for deadlock or for a serialization failure — so the application must detect aborts and retry them, which is the very thing many frameworks fail to do by default. Under serial execution the change is larger still: the transaction has to be submitted whole as a stored procedure. Predictable p99 is achievable, but only by choosing the implementation whose cost shows up as aborts rather than as waiting. (c) Contention on the hot set — how many concurrent transactions touch the same rows, and how long each read/write transaction stays open. That single property flips the answer: with low contention and spare capacity, optimistic concurrency control outperforms pessimistic; with high contention it collapses into abort storms while 2PL merely queues. Measure the concurrent access rate to the hot rows, the duration distribution of read/write transactions, and current headroom. Also worth measuring: whether the long reads can be moved onto a snapshot outside the serializable workload, which improves every option, and whether contention can be reduced by expressing hot updates as commutative atomic operations.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 1 — the deploy that took out unrelated features
questions.prompt: An order service writes to a relational database and publishes to a message broker from different vendors. To avoid publishing orders that were never persisted, the team wraps both in a distributed transaction using the standard cross-technology protocol, with the coordinator running as a library inside the order service. During a deploy, several order-service pods are killed mid-transaction. Within minutes, unrelated parts of the product start timing out, and the incident lasts far longer than the deploy. (a) Name the state those transactions are in and explain precisely why a timeout cannot resolve it. (b) Explain the mechanism by which killing an order-service pod caused unrelated features to fail, and say why restarting the databases would not have helped. (c) Name the escape hatch an operator might reach for, and state exactly what it costs.
questions.ideal: (a) Those transactions are in doubt (uncertain): each participant received a prepare request and voted yes, which surrendered its right to abort, and then lost the coordinator before hearing the decision. A timeout cannot resolve it because the participant has no information about the outcome — if it unilaterally aborts it may end up inconsistent with a participant that committed, and if it unilaterally commits it may end up inconsistent with one that aborted. Participants could in principle poll each other, but that is not part of the protocol. The only correct resolution is to wait for the coordinator to recover and read its log, which is exactly why the coordinator writes its decision to disk before sending anything. (b) Because a transaction holds row-level exclusive locks on everything it modified (and, under two-phase locking, shared locks on everything it read) until it commits or aborts — so an in-doubt transaction holds its locks for the entire time it is in doubt. Any other transaction touching those rows blocks, and depending on the isolation level may be blocked even from reading them, so features with no connection to orders stop working. Restarting the databases does not help: a correct implementation must preserve an in-doubt transaction's locks across restarts, because releasing them would risk violating atomicity. The incident outlasted the deploy because the coordinator was a library inside the order-service process — when the pod died the coordinator died with it, and its log sits on that server's local disk, making that disk part of the durable system state. (c) A heuristic decision: many implementations of the cross-technology standard let a participant unilaterally commit or abort an in-doubt transaction without a decision from the coordinator. The cost, stated plainly, is that "heuristic" is a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity — it violates the system of promises the protocol rests on, so participants can end up disagreeing permanently. It exists for catastrophes, not for routine recovery.

questions.prompt: Following that incident, an architect proposes: "distributed transactions are fundamentally broken — we should ban two-phase commit across the company." Another engineer objects that the company's new sharded database uses two-phase commit internally for every cross-shard write and has been entirely reliable. The team also still needs the guarantee that a message is processed exactly once. (a) Adjudicate: state the distinction the proposed ban misses, and give three concrete things the reliable case can do that the failed one cannot. (b) Design the exactly-once processing without any cross-technology atomic commit, and say what each step protects against. (c) Say what property your design actually achieves, and name one thing internal distributed transactions would still buy you.
questions.ideal: (a) The ban conflates two different things. Database-internal distributed transactions have participants all running the same software; heterogeneous ones span different technologies and must interoperate through a standard. Three concrete things the internal case can do: replicate the coordinator, with automatic failover to another coordinator node — commonly using a consensus algorithm — so a single crash doesn't leave anyone in doubt; let the coordinator and shards communicate directly, without going through application code, which removes the application as a single point of failure; and couple atomic commitment to a real concurrency-control protocol, giving cross-shard deadlock detection and consistent reads across shards. A fourth: replicate the participating shards so a fault in one doesn't force an abort. The heterogeneous case can do none of these, because it is a lowest common denominator — it cannot even detect deadlocks across systems, and it does not work with serializable snapshot isolation, since both would need standardised cross-system protocols. (b) Use only database-local transactions. 1. Give every message a unique ID and keep a table of processed IDs; on receiving a message, begin a transaction and check for the ID — if present, acknowledge and drop, which protects against a redelivery of something already done. 2. If absent, insert it, do the processing and its database writes in the same transaction, and commit — so a crash before commit aborts everything and the broker redelivers safely. 3. Acknowledge to the broker only after the commit succeeds — so a crash between commit and acknowledgment leads to a redelivery that step 1 will drop. 4. Delete the ID afterwards, in a separate transaction — a crash here leaves a stale row that costs a little storage and nothing else. A uniqueness constraint on the ID table covers the remaining case, where a retry arrives while the first attempt is still open: both cannot insert the same ID. (c) It achieves idempotence — processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once — and idempotence is what delivers exactly-once semantics here. Atomicity across the broker and the database was never actually required. What internal distributed transactions would still buy: scalability of this same pattern, letting the message-ID table live on one shard and the data updated by processing live on others, with atomic commit across those shards.

questions.prompt: Explain why ACID atomicity would have been better named abortability, and say which letter covers a concurrent client seeing your half-finished work.
questions.ideal: Because ACID atomicity is not about breaking something into indivisible parts, and it is not the multithreaded sense of the word at all. It describes what happens when a fault occurs after some of a transaction's writes have been processed — a crash, an interrupted connection, a full disk, a violated constraint: the transaction is aborted and every write it made so far is discarded. The value of that is precisely that the application can be sure nothing changed, so the operation can safely be retried. Abortability names that property; atomicity names something else. The letter covering a concurrent client seeing your half-finished work is I, for isolation.

questions.prompt: Give the two guarantees of read committed and how each is implemented — including the implementation that is possible but works badly, and exactly why it does.
questions.ideal: Read committed guarantees no dirty reads — you see only data that has been committed — and no dirty writes — you overwrite only data that has been committed. Dirty writes are prevented with row-level locks: a transaction wanting to modify a row must acquire the lock and hold it until it commits or aborts, so a second writer waits. Dirty reads are most commonly prevented without locks at all: for every row being written the database remembers both the old committed value and the new uncommitted one, and serves other readers the old value until the writer commits. The implementation that is possible but works badly is using the same lock for reads — requiring every reader to briefly acquire and release it. It is correct, and some databases do it, but one long-running write transaction then forces many read-only transactions to wait, so a slowdown in one part of an application shows up in a completely unrelated part.

questions.prompt: Explain read skew with a concrete example, say why nothing that was read was uncommitted, and name two workloads for which it is intolerable.
questions.ideal: Read skew, also called a nonrepeatable read, is seeing different parts of the database at different points in time. Example: $1,000 split across two accounts holding $500 each, with a $100 transfer in flight. You read one account before the incoming payment arrives and see $500, and the other after the outgoing transfer and see $400, so the total looks like $900 and $100 appears to have vanished. Nothing read was uncommitted: both balances were genuinely committed at the moment they were read, which is exactly why read committed permits this by design. Two workloads for which it is intolerable: taking a backup, which may run for hours while writes continue, so parts of the backup are older than others and the inconsistency becomes permanent if you restore from it; and analytical queries or periodic integrity checks that scan large parts of the database, which return nonsensical results if they observe different points in time.

questions.prompt: Describe how MVCC gives a transaction a consistent snapshot: what is tagged on each row, what an update really is, and the two-clause rule for whether a row is visible.
questions.ideal: Every transaction is given a unique, always-increasing transaction id when it starts, and everything it writes is tagged with that id. Each row carries an inserted_by field holding the id of the transaction that created it and a deleted_by field, initially empty, set to the id of a transaction that deletes it — the row is not removed, only marked, and a garbage collector reclaims it once no transaction can still see it. An update is internally a delete plus an insert, so several versions of the same row sit side by side, linked so a query can walk them. The two-clause visibility rule: a row is visible if the transaction that inserted it had already committed at the time the reader's transaction started, and the row is either not marked for deletion or the transaction that requested the deletion had not committed at that time. Equivalently, in rule form: ignore writes by transactions that were in progress when you started even if they later commit, ignore writes by transactions with a later id, ignore writes by aborted transactions, and everything else is visible.

questions.prompt: Name all five ways to prevent a lost update, and say what the fifth assumes that the other four do not.
questions.ideal: Atomic write operations, where the database performs the update itself and there is no read-modify-write cycle in application code. Explicit locking by the application, taking a lock on the rows it is about to depend on so concurrent cycles serialise — with deadlock as the attendant risk. Automatic detection of lost updates, letting the cycles run in parallel and aborting the loser so it retries, which composes efficiently with snapshot isolation and cannot be forgotten by the developer. Conditional writes, or compare-and-set, applying the update only if the value has not changed since it was read — including the version-number variant sometimes called optimistic locking. And in replicated systems, conflict resolution after the fact: allowing concurrent writes to create conflicting versions and merging them. What the fifth assumes that the others do not: the first four all assume there is a single up-to-date copy of the data, which multi-leader and leaderless replication cannot provide. Merging only prevents lost updates where the operations are commutative — incrementing a counter or adding to a set are, a conditional write is not — and last-write-wins, the default in many replicated databases, is itself prone to lost updates.

questions.prompt: Define write skew, say why it is the general case of the lost update, and name two lost-update preventions that do not work against it.
questions.ideal: Write skew occurs when two transactions read the same objects and then update some of those objects, with the two transactions updating different objects, so that together they violate an invariant neither broke alone. The canonical case: two on-call doctors each check that at least two doctors are on call, both see two, and each takes only themselves off call. It is the general case because a lost update is what you get in the special case where the different transactions update the same object — then the second write clobbers the first, giving a lost update or a dirty write depending on the timing. Two lost-update preventions that do not work against it: atomic single-object write operations, because multiple objects are involved; and the automatic lost-update detection built into some snapshot isolation implementations, which does not detect write skew at the equivalent levels of the major products. Preventing write skew automatically requires true serializable isolation.

questions.prompt: Explain what a phantom is and why an explicit lock on the rows you read cannot help, then give the remaining options and say which is preferred.
questions.ideal: A phantom is the effect where a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another. The pattern is: a SELECT checks whether a requirement holds by searching for rows matching a condition, the application decides based on the answer, and then it writes — and the write changes the set of rows matching that condition, so re-running the SELECT afterwards would give a different result. An explicit lock on the rows you read cannot help when the query checked for the absence of matching rows: if the query returned nothing, SELECT FOR UPDATE has nothing to attach a lock to. The remaining options are, first, a constraint where one fits — a plain uniqueness constraint solves the username case outright by aborting the second transaction; second, materialising the conflict, by pre-creating rows that exist solely to be locked, which turns the phantom into an ordinary lock conflict; and third, a serializable isolation level, which is what predicate locks and their index-range approximation were invented for. Serializable is preferred: materialising conflicts is hard and error-prone to work out and it leaks a concurrency-control mechanism into the data model, so it is a last resort when nothing else is possible.

questions.prompt: Name the three implementations of serializability and give the specific workload that defeats each one.
questions.ideal: Actual serial execution — run one transaction at a time on a single thread, which is serializable by definition. Defeated by write throughput above one CPU core, and by long transactions, since one slow transaction stalls all processing; it also needs the active dataset in memory and transactions submitted whole as stored procedures. Sharding gives a thread per core, but any transaction spanning shards must run in lockstep across them and cross-shard throughput is orders of magnitude lower and does not improve by adding machines. Two-phase locking — shared and exclusive locks held until the transaction ends, extended by predicate or index-range locks so it also prevents phantoms. Defeated by contention: concurrency is reduced by design, latency is unstable and very poor at high percentiles, deadlocks are far more frequent than at weak levels and each one discards a transaction's work, and a transaction reading a whole table takes a shared lock on the table so writes to it stop. Serializable snapshot isolation — snapshot isolation plus commit-time detection of transactions that acted on a premise that has since expired. Defeated by high contention, where the abort rate climbs and the retries add load to a system already near its maximum throughput; long read/write transactions are likely to conflict and abort, though long read-only ones are fine.

questions.prompt: State the two points of no return in two-phase commit, say what each one surrenders, and explain why a participant in doubt may not decide for itself.
questions.ideal: The first point of no return is a participant's yes vote in the prepare phase. Before answering, the participant must make sure it can definitely commit under all circumstances — writing all the transaction's data to disk and checking for conflicts and constraint violations — so a crash, a power failure or a full disk is no longer an acceptable excuse for refusing later. What it surrenders is the right to abort, without actually committing. The second is the moment the coordinator writes its decision to its own transaction log on disk; that write is the commit point, and it surrenders the right to change the decision. After it, the commit or abort request must be sent and retried forever until it succeeds. A participant in doubt — one that voted yes and then lost contact with the coordinator — may not decide for itself because it has no information about the outcome: unilaterally aborting after a timeout risks ending up inconsistent with a participant that committed, and unilaterally committing risks the reverse. Participants could in principle ask each other how they voted, but that is not part of the protocol, so the only way to complete is to wait for the coordinator to recover and read its log.

questions.prompt: Design exactly-once message processing without atomic commit across the broker and the database, and say what property it actually achieves.
questions.ideal: Use only transactions inside the database, and make the processing idempotent. Give every message a unique ID and keep a table of processed message IDs. On receiving a message, begin a database transaction and check the ID: if it is already present the message has been processed, so acknowledge it to the broker and drop it — this protects against a redelivery of work already done. If it is absent, insert it, process the message including any further database writes in the same transaction, and commit — so a crash before the commit aborts everything and the broker safely redelivers. Acknowledge to the broker only after the database transaction has committed — so a crash between committing and acknowledging leads to a redelivery that the first step drops. Then delete the ID in a separate transaction — a crash here leaves a stale ID that costs a little storage and nothing else. A uniqueness constraint on the ID table covers the remaining case, where a retry begins before the first attempt's transaction has aborted: two concurrent transactions cannot insert the same ID. What this achieves is idempotence — processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once — and idempotence is what delivers exactly-once semantics here. Atomicity across the broker and the database was never required. Internal distributed transactions remain useful for the scalability of this pattern, letting the message IDs live on one shard and the processed data on others.

competencies.title: Browser Networking — Latency, HTTP/1.x, Server-Sent Events, WebSocket

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 1 — the Sydney dashboard and the uplink upgrade
questions.prompt: A team's dashboard takes 4.2 seconds to become interactive for users in Sydney, against 1.1 seconds in London where the servers are. The page makes 78 requests. Someone proposes upgrading the origin's uplink from 1 Gbps to 10 Gbps, arguing that the origin is "clearly saturated" because Sydney is four times slower. (a) Explain, in terms of the four delays, why the Sydney figure is what it is and why the uplink upgrade will not help. (b) Estimate the floor: state the round-trip time you would expect and the arithmetic that gets you there, and say what the 78 requests do to it. (c) Give the two structurally different fixes available, say which delay each attacks, and name the one thing that would genuinely lower the floor and why nobody does it.
questions.ideal: (a) The Sydney figure is dominated by propagation delay, which is distance divided by signal speed and has nothing to do with anyone's link capacity. Upgrading the origin uplink reduces transmission delay — the time to push bits onto the wire — which is a function of the link's data rate and is independent of distance. Those are different delays with different causes, and the evidence in the question already rules out saturation: London, on the same origin and the same uplink, is fine. If the origin were saturated both would be slow. The remaining two delays, processing and queuing, also grow along the longer route because there are more hops, each reading headers and each with its own buffer. (b) The floor: New York to Sydney is 15,993 km and gives 160 ms round trip along the great circle, and the real figure over existing cables is 200–300 ms; London to Sydney is a comparable order of magnitude. Take a round trip of roughly 250 ms. The arithmetic is distance ÷ ~200,000 km/s for the one-way time in fibre, doubled — noting that fibre is about 1.5× slower than light in a vacuum. The 78 requests are what turn that into 4.2 seconds: each round trip is spent serially unless the requests overlap, and with six connections per host and no multiplexing they overlap only six at a time. That is roughly thirteen sequential batches of 250 ms before you count server time — which lands in the right neighbourhood. Credit for observing that users are already past the 1,000 ms mark at which they mentally context-switch. (c) Two structurally different fixes. Reduce the number of round trips — fewer resources, caching so repeat visits skip requests entirely, bundling, keepalive — which attacks how many times you pay the propagation delay, not the delay itself. And move the data closer with a CDN, which attacks the propagation delay directly and is the only lever on it. The thing that would genuinely lower the floor is a shorter cable along the great circle — and nobody does it here because laying cable is constrained by terrain, politics and cost, and is only justified where milliseconds are worth millions. Also creditable: better fibre and faster routers would help, but we are within about 1.5× of light speed so the ceiling on that strategy is roughly 30%.

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 2 — the gateway that never drops a packet
questions.prompt: An office reports that video calls became choppy and web browsing became erratic after the IT team replaced the gateway with a model advertising "zero packet loss under load". Throughput tests still show the full contracted line speed. The team's conclusion is that the provider must be throttling. (a) Name the most likely cause and explain the mechanism, including why the throughput test looks fine. (b) Explain precisely why a design goal of never dropping packets makes things worse rather than better. (c) Name the class of solution, and separately say why moving the video server closer would not fix this particular problem.
questions.ideal: (a) Bufferbloat. The new gateway ships with large incoming buffers on the assumption that dropping packets should be avoided at all costs. When arrivals outpace service, packets are queued rather than dropped, and the time they spend in that buffer is queuing delay — which is high and, critically, variable. Throughput looks fine because bufferbloat is not a capacity problem: every byte still arrives, and a throughput test measures exactly that. It measures the wrong quantity for this fault. (b) Because TCP's congestion avoidance uses packet loss as its signal. A dropped packet is how the network tells a sender to slow down. A buffer that absorbs the overflow suppresses that signal, so senders keep increasing their rate while the queue grows, and instead of a prompt backoff you get a long and unpredictable queue in front of every packet. The design goal is well-intentioned and the mechanism it breaks is the one that was keeping latency bounded — which is why the fix is not a bigger or a smaller buffer but a smarter one. (c) The class of solution is active queue management — algorithms that deliberately manage queue delay rather than maximising buffer occupancy; the CoDel algorithm was proposed for exactly this and is available in modern kernels. Moving the video server closer would not fix it because a CDN reduces propagation delay, and the delay here is queuing delay being introduced by a device inside the office, after the packet has already arrived. Shortening the journey does nothing about a queue at the destination.

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 1 — the dashboard whose fourth chart never loads
questions.prompt: A dashboard opens two Server-Sent Event streams and a long-lived polling request to api.example.com, then loads chart data from the same host. Users report that the fourth chart on the page never loads until they close a panel. A developer, seeing the streams are idle most of the time, argues they "cost nothing when no data is flowing" and proposes adding a fifth stream for notifications. (a) Name what is happening and explain the mechanism, including why the streams being idle is irrelevant. (b) Say what the underlying protocol limitation is and why the browser's behaviour here is a deliberate safety feature that has backfired. (c) Give two structurally different fixes, and say what each one costs.
questions.ideal: (a) The browser opens at most six connections per host, and the two event streams and the long-lived polling request occupy three of them permanently. With the chart requests competing for what remains, the seventh outstanding request to that host simply hangs until one of the earlier ones completes — which is why closing a panel unblocks it. Idleness is irrelevant because HTTP 1.x has no multiplexing: a connection carries one exchange at a time whether or not any bytes are moving, so a stream that has sent nothing for ten minutes is still holding a full TCP stream. (b) The underlying limitation is the absence of multiplexing, which is why browsers open several connections at all — and the per-host cap exists as a safety check, so that a client cannot saturate all available resources on a server, intentionally or otherwise. The irony is that the same check enables the reverse: exceed it on the client and all further requests to that host are blocked. Applications built on real-time delivery — sockets, event streams, hanging requests — are exactly the ones that hit it, so you can create a self-imposed denial of service against your own application. (c) Two structurally different fixes. Consolidate the streams: carry all the update types over one connection, distinguishing them by event type, so you spend one slot instead of three — costing you a shared failure domain and some multiplexing logic in the application. Or move the streams to a different hostname, so they draw against a separate connection pool — costing an extra DNS lookup, a fresh TCP slow-start, and possibly a fresh TLS handshake, all of which hit high-latency clients hardest. Also creditable: reduce the number of long-lived connections generally, and do not add the fifth.

questions.where: Part 2 · Question 2 — the bundle that helped desktop and hurt everything else
questions.prompt: A team bundles all 40 of its JavaScript modules into one 900 KB file and all 120 of its icons into one sprite sheet. Desktop metrics improved. Mobile metrics got worse, repeat-visit performance got worse, and one engineer reports the app being killed on older handsets. The team's proposal is to shard the bundle across four subdomains so it downloads in parallel. (a) Explain each of the three regressions in terms of what bundling actually trades away. (b) Say whether sharding addresses any of them, and justify the answer. (c) Give the changes you would make instead, and state what remains true regardless of protocol.
questions.ideal: (a) Three distinct trades. Mobile got worse because a 900 KB bundle must arrive in full before any of it executes — neither CSS nor JavaScript allows incremental execution — so on a high-latency, low-bandwidth link the time to first render is dominated by a transfer that used to be able to start executing in pieces. Repeat visits got worse because all 40 modules now share one cache key: a single change to any one of them invalidates and re-downloads the whole 900 KB. That is the loss of cache granularity, and it is the classic cost of bundling. The app is being killed because a sprite is decoded and held in memory as a bitmap at width × height × 4 bytes, regardless of the compressed file size and regardless of how little of it is on screen — the browser does not clip the unused part out of memory. (b) No, and it may make things worse. Sharding multiplies the per-host connection limit; it does not reduce bytes, does not restore cache granularity, and does not reduce memory. It cannot even parallelise this download, because one 900 KB resource is a single request and lives on a single connection. What it does add is a DNS lookup and a fresh TCP slow-start per shard, which penalises exactly the high-latency mobile clients that are already the problem. (c) Split the bundle: separate the stable core — frameworks and libraries that rarely change — from volatile application code, so a routine change invalidates only a small bundle; target roughly 30–50 KB compressed per script bundle, large enough to amortise per-request overhead and small enough to allow incremental execution; deliver first-paint-critical CSS separately from the rest. Stop spriting the icons at that scale, and inline only the small, page-specific ones — roughly under 1–2 KB, remembering base64 costs 33% and an inlined asset cannot be cached separately. What remains true regardless of protocol: eliminate unnecessary latency and minimise transferred bytes. Bundling and sharding are workarounds for a protocol that cannot interleave responses; caching, compression and deleting resources are not.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 1 — the price stream with a gap after every reconnect
questions.prompt: A trading desk streams price updates to browsers over Server-Sent Events. Every client reconnects roughly every 60 seconds, and after each reconnect traders see a gap in the tape. The stream also carries small chart images, base64-encoded into the data field, and the mobile app's battery consumption has become a complaint. The team's proposed fix is a heartbeat message every 5 seconds to "keep the connection from dropping". (a) Explain the gap: say what the browser does on reconnect and precisely where the responsibility for the missing messages lies. (b) Diagnose the 60-second reconnect cycle and say why the proposed heartbeat is the wrong fix and what it will cost. (c) Give the correct handling for the chart images, with the cost of your approach and two things it buys back.
questions.ideal: (a) On reconnect the browser does two things automatically: it reestablishes the connection after the retry interval, and if the server has been assigning IDs it sends the last one it saw back as a Last-Event-ID header. That is the whole of the browser's contribution. Replaying the missed messages is entirely the server's job — it must maintain a local cache of recent events and, on seeing that header, retransmit everything after that ID. A gap after every reconnect means either the server is not sending IDs at all, so the client has nothing to report, or it is sending them and ignoring the header on reconnect. Either way the browser is behaving exactly as designed. (b) A reconnect cycle at a suspiciously round 60 seconds points at an idle or read timeout in the infrastructure — a proxy, load balancer or server tuned for short bursty HTTP rather than long-lived streams — or at an intermediary buffering the stream. The heartbeat is the wrong fix because it treats a configuration problem as a protocol problem: it does not raise anyone's timeout, it merely keeps traffic flowing so the timeout is not reached, which is a workaround that has to keep working forever. Its cost is paid by the mobile clients: a message every 5 seconds wakes the radio continuously, which is exactly the real-time push anti-pattern that drains handset batteries, and an SSE connection is not dropped merely because the radio has gone idle. The right sequence is: raise the timeouts you control, put the stream over TLS so intermediaries cannot buffer it, and batch real messages instead of manufacturing filler ones. (c) Stop base64-encoding the charts into the stream. The stream is UTF-8 only by design, so binary costs a 33% byte expansion, and a streamed asset cannot be cached by the browser cache at all. Instead use the stream as a notification: push a small text message saying a new chart exists and where, and let the application fetch it with an ordinary request. The cost is one extra round trip per image. What it buys back: the asset becomes cacheable by the browser and by any intermediary, and it gets ordinary transfer encoding and compression — plus the 33% goes away.
