Also creditable: gzip the event stream itself, which is legitimate because it is an ordinary HTTP response.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 2 — choosing a push transport for job progress
questions.prompt: A team is replacing 5-second polling with a push transport for a job-progress feature: the server emits short text status lines, and at the end a downloadable report. They are choosing between Server-Sent Events and a WebSocket. An architect argues for the WebSocket on the grounds that it "will be lower latency" and "we might want the client to send later". (a) Address the latency claim precisely, naming which latency changes and which does not. (b) Name three concrete things SSE gives them for free that they would have to build themselves on a socket. (c) Say how the final report should be delivered under your recommendation, and what would have to change for the WebSocket to become the right answer.
questions.ideal: (a) The claim is wrong as stated. Changing transport does not decrease the round trip between client and server at all — propagation latency is a function of distance and the speed of light and is identical for polling, a stream or a socket. What both persistent transports eliminate is queuing latency: with 5-second polling, a status line can be ready on the server and still wait up to 5 seconds for the next request, whereas a persistent connection lets the server dispatch it the moment it exists. SSE and WebSocket are identical on this axis for server-to-client data; the socket adds nothing here. It only differs for messages travelling the other way. (b) Three things SSE gives free that a socket does not. Automatic reconnection, at a default of 2–3 seconds and adjustable by the server with a retry field. Last-seen message tracking, where the browser remembers the ID and reports it on reconnect. And message parsing with no unbounded buffer — the browser finds the boundaries, extracts the payload and fires a DOM event per message, discarding what it has processed. Also creditable: session-wide gzip, which works because the stream is all text and an ordinary HTTP response; and the fact that it is ordinary HTTP, so it deploys through existing infrastructure with no new negotiation. (c) The report should be delivered as a notification on the stream plus an ordinary HTTP request to fetch it — one extra round trip, in exchange for a cacheable, compressible, resumable download that any intermediary can serve, and no base64 tax. The WebSocket becomes right when the client needs to send frequently and with low latency — live cancellation, parameter changes during the run, a cursor or control channel — or when the downward data becomes genuinely binary and high-volume. Reaching for it merely because the client might send later trades caching, compression, reconnection and last-ID tracking for a capability nobody is using yet.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 1 — the map that freezes when you pan
questions.prompt: A collaborative map application sends cursor positions and edits over a WebSocket, and also streams map tiles down the same socket as binary messages because "binary is free on a socket". Users report that cursors freeze for a second or two whenever the map is panned, and the operations team reports origin bandwidth roughly ten times what was forecast. The proposed fix is to increase the server's send buffer. (a) Name the mechanism behind the freezing cursors and say why a bigger send buffer will not fix it. (b) Explain the bandwidth figure — say precisely what stopped happening when the tiles moved onto the socket. (c) Give the redesign, name what each kind of traffic should travel over, and name one client-side check the application should be doing regardless.
questions.ideal: (a) Head-of-line blocking on the socket. Messages are delivered in exactly the order the client and server queue them, and although a message may be split into several frames, frames from different messages cannot be interleaved — there is no stream identifier in the framing layer. So a large tile message occupies the connection until it has been fully sent, and every cursor update queued behind it waits. A bigger send buffer makes it worse rather than better: it lets more large messages queue up ahead of the small ones, which is more of the same problem. The fix is at the application layer — split large messages, check what is already queued, and prioritise. (b) The tiles stopped being cacheable. Delivered as ordinary HTTP resources they are held by the browser cache, by any intermediary proxy, and by a CDN, so a panned-over tile is fetched once and a popular tile is served to thousands of users from an edge node. Streamed inside a custom protocol they are opaque: nothing in the middle can identify or store them, so every client fetches every tile every time and all of that traffic terminates at the origin. Roughly ten times the forecast is exactly what losing a cache hierarchy looks like. (c) Route by cacheability. Cursor positions, edits, presence and control messages go over the socket — genuinely non-cacheable, latency-sensitive, small, and needed in both directions. Tiles go over ordinary HTTP, fetched by the client, where they are cached by the browser and the CDN and compressed by ordinary negotiation; the socket can carry a message telling the client which tiles to fetch. The client-side check the application should be doing regardless is to monitor bufferedAmount before sending: send() is asynchronous and returns immediately, so a fast return is not evidence of delivery, and sending the next update only once the buffer has drained is what keeps a backlog from forming.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 2 — a third of clients never connect
questions.prompt: A team ships a WebSocket feature. It works in development. In production, roughly a third of clients never establish a connection at all, and of those that do, many silently die after about a minute. Mobile users are worst affected. The team is on plain ws:// behind a proxy and a load balancer they operate, and their fallback is a polyfill library whose default transport is polling. (a) Give the most likely cause of the failed connections and the mechanism, and name the single change that addresses most of them. (b) Explain the one-minute deaths and say exactly where to look, including the setting people most often miss. (c) Say why the polyfill is a performance risk rather than a safety net, and what the handshake's key-and-accept exchange does and does not protect against.
questions.ideal: (a) The most likely cause is intermediaries that do not understand the protocol — explicit and transparent proxies, firewalls and carrier equipment between the client and the server. Because the connection begins as an HTTP Upgrade, such devices may blindly upgrade without understanding what they upgraded to, buffer frames, modify content, or misclassify the traffic as a compromised HTTP connection and drop it. Mobile clients are worst affected because their traffic crosses the most such equipment. The single change that addresses most of it is to use the secure scheme: negotiating TLS before the Upgrade handshake creates an end-to-end tunnel that intermediaries cannot inspect or alter, and in practice it significantly raises the success rate of establishing the session. Some networks block this traffic outright, which is why a fallback is still needed. (b) Deaths at about a minute are idle timeouts in infrastructure the team operates. HTTP is optimised for short bursty transfers, so proxies, load balancers and servers are routinely configured to time out idle connections aggressively — one widely used proxy defaults to 60 seconds — and that is exactly wrong for a long-lived session. Raise the read and write timeouts explicitly on the proxy. The setting most often missed is on the load balancer: its connect, client and server timeouts apply only to the initial HTTP Upgrade handshake, and once the upgrade completes the connection is governed by a separate tunnel timeout that has to be raised on its own. Note also that TLS does not help here — it improves the odds of establishing the session but does not stop anyone timing out an idle TCP connection. (c) The polyfill is a performance risk because the hard part of emulation is not the API but the transport: the fallbacks are polling, long-polling or a streaming request, and the library's choice decides what a fallen-back client actually experiences — polling reintroduces both the queuing latency and the full per-request HTTP overhead the socket existed to remove. Always prefer the native interface and hold the fallback to the same performance goals. The key-and-accept exchange in the handshake is a security policy against blind upgrades: it proves the server genuinely understands the requested protocol version rather than having switched protocols without knowing what it switched to. It does not authenticate anyone, does not encrypt anything, and does not protect against a transparent proxy that analyses and modifies data on the wire without announcing itself — which is precisely why the answer to (a) is a tunnel.

questions.prompt: Name the four components of latency, say what each is a function of, and name the only one that more bandwidth reduces.
questions.ideal: Propagation delay — the time for a message to travel from sender to receiver, a function of distance over the speed the signal propagates; in fibre roughly 200,000 km per second, a refractive index of about 1.5. Transmission delay — the time to push all the packet's bits onto the link, a function of the packet's length and the link's data rate, and independent of distance. Processing delay — the time to examine the packet header, check for bit-level errors and determine the outgoing route, incurred at every hop and now largely done in hardware. Queuing delay — the time the packet spends waiting in a router's incoming buffer before it can be processed, which grows with load. The total is the sum of all four at every hop. The only one more bandwidth reduces is transmission delay: a 10 Mb file takes 10 seconds to put on the wire at 1 Mbps and 0.1 seconds at 100 Mbps.

questions.prompt: Explain why latency and bandwidth have different futures, giving the physical reason and the approximate ceiling on improving latency.
questions.ideal: Bandwidth is an engineering and economic problem with no fundamental wall. You can add more fibres to a link, deploy more links along congested routes, or improve the wavelength-division multiplexing so more channels share the fibre you already have — and in practice much of the recent capacity growth came from better equipment at both ends of existing cable rather than new cable, with a large share of deployed subsea capacity still unused. Every medium eventually reaches diminishing returns, but there is no reason throughput cannot keep rising. Latency is different because the speed of light is a hard physical limit on propagation, and packets already travel through fibre at within roughly 1.5 times that limit. Better materials with a lower refractive index and faster routers could close some of that gap, but the ceiling on the whole strategy is a modest improvement of about 30 percent. The only other lever is to make the distance shorter — laying cable closer to the great-circle path, or moving the servers nearer the users — and laying new cable is constrained by terrain, politics and cost.

questions.prompt: Explain bufferbloat: what the designers were trying to achieve, what mechanism it breaks, and why a throughput test looks fine.
questions.ideal: The designers were trying to avoid dropping packets, on the assumption that loss should be prevented at all costs, and so shipped routers with very large incoming buffers. What it breaks is TCP's congestion avoidance, which relies on loss: a dropped packet is the network's way of telling a sender to back off. A buffer big enough to swallow the overflow removes that notification, so the sending rate keeps climbing while the queue lengthens, and the outcome is queuing delay that is both large and — the part that matters — unpredictable from moment to moment. A throughput test looks fine because bufferbloat is not a capacity problem: every byte still arrives, and throughput is exactly what the test measures. It is measuring the wrong quantity for the fault. The fix is not a bigger or smaller buffer but active queue management, which manages queue delay directly; the CoDel algorithm was proposed for this and is available in modern kernels.

questions.prompt: Give the latency saving from connection reuse as a formula, and say why the fixed cost of a new connection matters more the faster your server is.
questions.ideal: The saving is (N − 1) × RTT across N requests on one connection. Without keepalive every request costs two round trips — one for the TCP three-way handshake and one for the request-response cycle. With keepalive only the first request pays the handshake; every subsequent one costs a single round trip, because the connection is reused and another round of slow-start is avoided. With an average page now carrying ninety-odd resources, the potential saving is measured in seconds. The fixed cost matters more the faster the server is because it is fixed: the two round trips do not shrink when server processing time falls, so as the server's contribution approaches zero the protocol overhead approaches 100 percent of the time the user waits.

questions.prompt: Define head-of-line blocking in HTTP 1.x, and give three distinct reasons pipelining was abandoned in browsers.
questions.ideal: Head-of-line blocking in HTTP 1.x is the consequence of strict serialisation of responses: data from multiple responses cannot be interleaved on the same connection, so each response must be returned in full before the bytes of the next one can be transferred. If the server processes an HTML request and a CSS request in parallel and the CSS finishes first, the CSS response must be buffered until the HTML response has been sent — so a slow or hanging first response blocks everything behind it, giving underutilised links, server buffering costs and unpredictable client latency. Three distinct reasons pipelining was abandoned in browsers, from: a single slow response blocks all requests behind it; servers processing in parallel must buffer completed responses, and a very large one can exhaust server resources, which is an attack vector; a failed response may terminate the connection, forcing the client to re-request everything after it and possibly duplicating processing; detecting pipelining compatibility reliably is hard when intermediaries may be present; and some intermediaries abort the connection while others serialise every request.

questions.prompt: Explain why six connections per host can produce a denial of service against your own application, and why an idle stream is not free.
questions.ideal: Browsers open at most about six connections per host. That limit exists as a safety check so a client cannot saturate all the available resources on a server, intentionally or otherwise — but the same check enables the reverse attack on the client: once the limit is reached, all further requests to that host are blocked. Open six parallel downloads to one host and the seventh hangs until one completes. This becomes a real deployment problem for applications relying on real-time delivery, because a WebSocket, a Server-Sent Events stream or a hanging request each occupies a full TCP stream even while no data is being transferred — there is no multiplexing, so a connection carries one exchange at a time whether or not bytes are moving. Three idle long-lived connections therefore leave you three ordinary requests, and you have created a denial of service against your own application.

questions.prompt: Name one distinct cost each for domain sharding, bundling and inlining, and say which of the three would still make sense under a protocol that could interleave responses.
questions.ideal: Domain sharding: every additional hostname requires an extra DNS lookup, and each new connection starts in TCP slow-start, so overuse leaves many underutilised streams and can slow the experience down — and high-latency mobile clients pay both costs hardest. Bundling and spriting: you lose cache granularity, because all the combined resources live under one URL and cache key, so a single change to any one of them invalidates and re-downloads the whole bundle; also creditable are shipping resources this page does not need, holding a decoded sprite in memory in full at width × height × 4 bytes, and delaying execution because neither CSS nor JavaScript runs until the entire file has arrived. Inlining: the resource becomes part of the page and cannot be cached individually by the browser, a CDN or any proxy, so inlining it across several pages ships it with every one of them; also creditable is the 33 percent expansion base64 imposes on non-text assets. None of the three would make sense under a protocol that could interleave responses — all three exist to work around the lack of multiplexing and high per-request overhead, which is exactly what distinguishes them from the evergreen optimisations of eliminating unnecessary latency and minimising transferred bytes.

questions.prompt: Describe the Server-Sent Events wire format and say exactly which parts of the reconnect-and-recover story the browser handles and which you do.
questions.ideal: The wire format is a streaming HTTP response: the client makes an ordinary request advertising that it accepts an event stream, the server replies 200 with content type text/event-stream and chunked transfer encoding, and then keeps writing. The body is newline-delimited fields. data: carries the payload, and adjacent data lines are concatenated into one message rather than being separate messages. event: is an optional type, which makes a custom DOM event fire instead of the generic message callback. id: is an optional identifier. retry: sets the client's reconnect interval in milliseconds. Event boundaries are marked by newlines — a blank line ends the event — and that is the entire protocol. On reconnect the browser does two things: it reestablishes the connection automatically after the retry interval, with a recommended default of 2 to 3 seconds; and it remembers the ID of the last message it saw and sends it back as a Last-Event-ID header. Everything else is yours: if lost messages matter you must assign IDs to the relevant events and keep a server-side cache so you can retransmit everything after the reported ID, and you decide how far back to persist. If lost messages are acceptable, send no IDs and simply let the client resume.

questions.prompt: State which kind of latency a persistent connection removes and which it does not, then give SSE's two hard limits and the standard workaround for the second.
questions.ideal: A persistent connection removes queuing latency — the time a message that is ready on the server has to wait before it can be routed to the other party. With polling that wait is a function of the poll interval; with a persistent connection the server dispatches the message the moment it becomes available. It does not remove propagation latency: switching transports does not decrease the round trip between client and server at all, because that is distance over signal speed. Server-Sent Events has two hard limits. It is server-to-client only, so it does not address request streaming — the client cannot send data on the connection after the initial handshake. And the event-stream protocol is specifically designed for UTF-8 text, so binary streaming, while possible by base64-encoding, is inefficient and costs 33 percent in bytes. The standard workaround for the second is to resolve it at the application layer: the stream delivers a notification that a new binary asset is available, and the application dispatches an ordinary request to fetch it. That costs one extra round trip and buys back the services of a normal HTTP request — response caching, transfer encoding and compression — none of which a streamed asset can have, since a streamed asset cannot be cached by the browser cache.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a WebSocket frame from a message, and name three services you stop receiving once the connection has been upgraded.
questions.ideal: A frame is the smallest unit of communication on the wire: a variable-length frame header plus a payload that may carry all or part of an application message. A message is the complete sequence of frames that map to one logical application message. Whether to fragment a message into several frames is decided by the client's and server's framing code, and applications remain unaware of individual frames — the receiving callback is invoked only when the entire message is available, even for a very large payload. Three services you stop receiving once the connection has been upgraded, from: caching, because data delivered inside a custom protocol will not be cached by the browser cache or by any intermediary such as a CDN, so you may incur unnecessary transfers and much higher traffic to origin; automatic compression, because a WebSocket carries both text and binary so compressing the whole session makes no sense — the per-message compression extension was not broadly available, leaving it to the application; message metadata, because there is no equivalent of HTTP headers and only a single bit distinguishes text from binary, so client and server must agree their own subprotocol to carry it; and more generally state management and the other services the browser provides for HTTP. Also creditable: head-of-line blocking returns, since frames from different messages cannot be interleaved.

parts: Where you stand decides what you see
The numbers will lie to you

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 1 — the array that is “maxed out”
questions.prompt: A team reports that their storage tier is “maxed out”: the monitoring dashboard shows the array at 100% utilization all through the working day. They have quoted for a second array. Separately, users complain of slow requests only between 09:15 and 09:40 — a window in which the dashboard shows nothing unusual, because it plots five-minute averages. The array's own queue-length metric is not collected. (a) Explain why 100% utilization on the dashboard may not mean the array is out of capacity, and give the everyday example that makes the distinction. (b) Explain how the morning window can be a real problem that the dashboard cannot show, and name the metric that would settle it. (c) Say what you would collect before approving the purchase, and classify the missing queue-length metric in terms of what you know about your own knowledge.
questions.ideal: (a) The dashboard is almost certainly reporting time-based utilization — U = B/T, the fraction of the interval the resource was busy, which a disk tool would more honestly call percent busy. That is not the same as capacity-based utilization, the fraction of deliverable throughput in use. Storage arrays frequently run at 100% precisely because some disk is busy the whole time while the array as a whole has plenty of idle disks and can accept more work. The everyday example is a lift: it may be moving between floors 100% of the time and still have room for passengers. 100% busy does not mean 100% capacity. (b) The morning window can be real because an average conceals its interval. Five-minute averages mask short periods at 100%, and a short burst of high utilization is enough to cause saturation and a queue — the toll-plaza case, where a 40% daily average tells you nothing about whether anyone queued during rush hour. The metric that settles it is saturation, expressed as a wait-queue length or as time spent waiting, because unlike utilization it has no ambiguous form: any non-zero value is work that arrived and could not be serviced, which is latency someone experienced. (c) Collect the queue length (and errors) for the array, at a much shorter interval than five minutes, over the 09:15–09:40 window — that combination distinguishes “busy but coping” from “out of capacity”, and it is the pair the utilization figure cannot separate. The missing queue-length metric is a known-unknown: you know the metric exists and you have not observed it. Recording it as such is a result rather than a gap — it is precisely the kind of thing a tool-first approach would have left as an invisible blind spot. Credit for noting that a purchase justified by a number that cannot distinguish the two cases is unjustified.

questions.where: Part 1 · Question 2 — the cache, the forum tunable and the redundant work
questions.prompt: A service resizes images. Someone proposes adding an in-memory result cache and runs a ten-minute benchmark, which shows a 4% improvement; they conclude caching is not worth it. A colleague proposes instead a configuration change deep in the storage layer, found on a forum post, which they say gave someone else “a 3× speedup”. A third engineer notes that the service's own code re-reads and re-decodes the same source image several times per request. (a) Give two independent reasons the benchmark result is not evidence against the cache. (b) Assess the forum tunable, naming what it is and is not useful for. (c) Rank the three proposals and justify the ranking with the general principle about where tuning pays — including the caveat about where to observe from.
questions.ideal: (a) Two independent reasons. First, the cache was almost certainly cold for most of a ten-minute run: caches start cold and warm over time, and when the cache is large or the next tier slow, warming takes far longer than people expect — the worked case is a 128 GB memory cache filling at 16 MB/s and taking over two hours. A benchmark shorter than the warm-up measures the wrong thing. Second, the hit ratio's effect is strongly non-linear, so a partially warm cache sitting at a low ratio produces very little of the benefit a hot cache would: the difference between 98% and 99% is far larger than between 10% and 11%. Also creditable: the right figure to check is the miss rate, not the ratio, since the misses are what cost time. (b) It is a point-in-time recommendation. A tunable found elsewhere may be inappropriate for this system and workload, may have been appropriate once and not now, or may be a temporary workaround for a bug already fixed in a later version — the comparison drawn is with taking someone else's prescription medicine. What it is good for is discovering which parameters exist and have needed changing; your job then becomes deciding whether and how they should be tuned here. Note also that you may still miss an important parameter simply because nobody else has needed to change it. If adopted, it should be stored in version control with the reason and date. (c) Ranking: the redundant decoding first, then the cache, then the storage tunable. The principle is that tuning is most effective closest to where the work is performed — at the application level you can eliminate work entirely, for gains of the order of 20×, whereas tuning down at the storage device happens after the higher-level stack has already executed and yields percentages, of the order of 20%. Re-reading and re-decoding the same image is unnecessary work, and eliminating unnecessary work is the largest win available. The caveat: the most effective level to tune is not necessarily the most effective level from which to observe — the redundant decoding may be easiest to see from operating system tools showing file system and disk I/O, or time on-CPU, rather than from inside the application.

questions.prompt: An engineer is paged for slow checkout. Within ten minutes they have opened their usual dashboard, seen elevated disk activity, raised a ticket with the storage team, and gone back to other work. The storage team spends two days demonstrating the array is healthy. Meanwhile a second engineer changes three configuration values at once during the incident; performance improves and the changes are left in place. Nobody has yet asked the checkout team anything. (a) Name the methods being used by each engineer and state the feature they share. (b) Say what should have happened first, list what it would have established, and explain why it costs almost nothing. (c) Name two distinct problems created by the second engineer's approach, one of which will only appear much later.
questions.ideal: (a) The first engineer is using the streetlight anti-method — opening the tools they know and looking for something odd — followed by the blame-someone-else anti-method, redirecting to a team they are not on. The second is using the random change anti-method. What all three share, and the identifying feature to name, is that the hypothesis arrived before the data, or with no data behind it at all. Note also the first engineer's specific failure: elevated disk activity may be an issue, but nothing in the approach quantified it, so there is no basis for believing it is the issue. (b) The problem statement should have come first, since it is the method to attempt before any other on a new issue. Its six questions: what makes you think there is a performance problem; has this system ever performed well; what changed recently, in software, hardware or load; can the problem be expressed in terms of latency or runtime; does it affect other people or applications; and what is the environment, with software, hardware, versions and configuration. It costs almost nothing because it requires no tools, no access and no metrics — issues have been resolved this way over the phone without logging in to any server. In this scenario the third question alone would likely have identified a recent change, and nobody has yet asked it. (c) Two problems. First, changing three values at once destroys attribution: they cannot know which change mattered, and the discipline is to reverse a change that does not work before forming the next hypothesis, precisely because changing multiple factors at once makes it impossible to identify which one was responsible. Second, the one that appears later: they have left behind tuning nobody understood in the first place. If it happens to work around a bug in the database or operating system that is later fixed, the tuning remains, no longer makes sense, and nobody will dare remove it. Also creditable: a poorly understood change can cause a worse problem at peak production load, requiring an emergency rollback.

questions.prompt: A platform team maintains a 30-entry checklist, built over two years, that every engineer runs on any performance complaint. It is fast and frequently effective. This quarter it has failed three times: twice it reported nothing while users were clearly affected, and once it recommended a tunable change that made things worse. The team's proposal is to add more entries and to buy two more observability tools. (a) Say what the checklist is good for and name its two structural limitations. (b) Explain why adding tools addresses the wrong constraint, and name the specific blind spot the tools-oriented approach has. (c) Give the sequence you would put in front of the checklist, and say what should be recorded when a question turns out to be unanswerable.
questions.ideal: (a) The checklist is genuinely valuable: an ad hoc checklist can provide the most value in the shortest time frame, and it is an effective way to ensure a whole team knows how to check for common issues, written clearly and prescriptively. Its two structural limitations: every entry is a point-in-time recommendation that needs frequent refreshing to stay current — which explains the tunable that made things worse — and checklists skew toward issues with known, easily documented fixes, typically tunable settings, rather than custom fixes to source code or the environment. That explains the two silent failures. (b) Adding tools deepens the tools method, which relies exclusively on the tools you have or know and therefore gives an incomplete view of the system. The specific blind spot, and the reason it is dangerous rather than merely limited, is that the user is unaware that the view is incomplete — and may remain unaware. Issues requiring custom tooling may never be identified. It also scales badly: with many tools of overlapping functionality, time goes into evaluating which to use rather than into the investigation. (c) Put the problem statement first on every issue, then a hypothesis-driven loop — the scientific method (question, hypothesis, prediction, test, analysis) or the tighter diagnosis cycle (hypothesis → instrumentation → data → hypothesis), moving to data quickly so bad theories are discarded early. Where a resource sweep is wanted, prefer the USE method, because it iterates over resources rather than tools: you build the complete list of questions first and only then look for something that can answer them. And the answer to the last part: a question you cannot answer should be recorded as a known-unknown. Knowing which questions are unanswered is extremely useful, and it is exactly the information a tool-first approach conceals.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 1 — the payments service that slowed over three weeks
questions.prompt: A payments service has slowed down over three weeks. Latency at the 99th percentile has tripled; the request rate is unchanged. An engineer has spent two days profiling application code and found nothing conclusive. The service runs in a container with a memory cap; the host is comfortably provisioned and its dashboards look calm. Nobody has looked at the service since it was deployed eleven months ago. (a) Using the rate-and-duration relationship, say what class of problem this is and what it rules out. (b) Name the method you would run first, give its three metrics in the correct order with the reason for that order, and say specifically how you would apply it to a capped container — including why the calm host is not reassuring. (c) Name one further method that is cheap, requires no load, and is very likely to be relevant given the last sentence of the scenario.
questions.ideal: (a) Duration has risen while the request rate is unchanged, which points at the architecture — the service itself — rather than at load. That is the distinction the request rate buys you: if both rate and duration had risen, the problem might be the load applied, and the investigation would go to workload characterization. Here it rules that out early, before any deep analysis. (b) Run the USE method: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. The order is errors first, because they are usually objective rather than subjective and so are quick to interpret and time-efficient to rule out; saturation second, because it is quicker to interpret than utilization and any level of it can be an issue; utilization last. For a capped container, apply the same three questions to the resource controls rather than only to the physical hardware: memory capacity utilization is the tenant's usage against its cap, and memory capacity saturation shows up as limit-imposed allocation errors or swapping for that tenant even when the host system is not experiencing memory pressure. That is exactly why the calm host dashboards are not reassuring — they are measuring the wrong boundary. (c) Static performance tuning: check the configured architecture with no load applied, asking of each component whether it makes sense, whether its configuration suits the intended workload, whether it was auto-configured into the best state, and whether it has degraded after an error. Eleven months without review is exactly the situation it exists for — a negotiated-down network interface, a failed disk in a redundant pool, an old version, a nearly-full file system, a debug mode accidentally left enabled. These are easy to check for; the hard part is remembering to do it. Also creditable: baseline statistics, or failing that summary-since-boot values, to establish whether current figures are normal for this server.

questions.where: Part 3 · Question 2 — the reporting database and the hanging queries
questions.prompt: A reporting database is slow every weekday morning. Average query latency looks acceptable, but users describe some queries as “hanging”. The team has confirmed the hardware is healthy and the query plans are unchanged since last year, and is now proposing to double the number of database instances. No one has examined which clients are connecting or what they are asking for. (a) Name the method that addresses the gap in the last sentence, give its four questions, and say why they should be asked even when the team is confident of the answers. (b) The average latency is acceptable and some queries hang. Name the method that resolves that contradiction and explain what it looks at that a summary cannot. (c) Before doubling the instances, name what must be established, and give the ordering principle that says where to look for a fix first.
questions.ideal: (a) Workload characterization, which focuses on the input to the system rather than the resulting performance. Its four questions: who is causing the load (process, user, remote address), why is it being called (code path, stack trace), what are its characteristics (rate, throughput, direction, type — with variance where appropriate), and how is it changing over time (is there a daily pattern). They should be asked even when the team is confident because you may be surprised: the worked example is a team who checked the client addresses of a database they expected to be used by their web servers, and discovered the entire internet was sending load — a denial-of-service attack. A weekday-morning pattern is itself a strong hint that the fourth question matters here. (b) Event tracing. Summaries such as an average latency destroy exactly the detail that matters when a small number of operations behave very differently from the rest; tracing inspects events individually, recording for each the input (type, direction, size), the times (start, end, latency) and the result (error status, transfer size). It also surfaces something no summary can: a latency outlier may be caused by preceding events rather than by its own properties — an event at the tail of a queue is slow because of what was queued ahead of it. Also creditable: the distribution is probably multimodal, so the average is not an index of central tendency, and a histogram or heat map would show the modes. (c) Before adding capacity you must establish whether this is a problem of load or of architecture — adding instances is the correct response to load, and does nothing for a single-threaded bottleneck or lock contention. The ordering principle is the performance mantras, most effective first: don't do it (eliminate unnecessary work); do it but don't do it again (caching); do it less (reduce refresh or polling frequency); do it later (write-back); do it when they're not looking (schedule off-peak); do it concurrently; and only last, do it more cheaply — buy faster hardware. Doubling the instances is the last item on that list, being proposed first. For a weekday-morning peak, “do it when they're not looking” is a particularly live option.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 1 — the storage that is “healthy”
questions.prompt: A team reports that their storage is healthy: mean I/O latency is 3.2 ms against a 10 ms target, device utilization averages 55%, and the 99th percentile is 12 ms. Users of one feature report frequent multi-second stalls. The team's dashboard shows five-minute averages, and their conclusion is that the application must be at fault. (a) Give two independent reasons the 3.2 ms mean may be consistent with users experiencing stalls, naming the phenomenon in each case. (b) Address the 55% utilization figure directly, with the queueing result and the reason it applies more forcefully to disks than to CPUs. (c) Say what you would ask for instead of these three numbers, and name the visualization you would use and why it beats the alternatives at this scale.
questions.ideal: (a) Two independent reasons. First, a multimodal distribution: system performance is frequently bimodal — a fast path and a slow one, or on-disk cache hits and misses — and the mean then falls in the gap between the modes. In the worked case, modes under 1 ms and near 7 ms give a mean of 3.3 ms, which is not an index of central tendency; it is almost the opposite, and describes nothing that actually happened. Second, outliers: a very small number of extreme values, such as occasional disk I/O over 1,000 ms among a majority between 0 and 10 ms. These barely move the mean, do not move the median at all, and are exactly what a user experiences as a multi-second stall. Whether the 99th percentile catches them depends on how frequent they are; a maximum may be the only summary that shows them. (b) 55% utilization is not the reassurance they think. Modelling the disk as M/D/1 gives r = s(2 − ρ)/2(1 − ρ), and beyond 60% utilization the mean response time has doubled; by 80% it has tripled. So they are already close to the point where queueing dominates, and this is the best case — variation in service time drives the mean higher still, and the 90th and 99th percentiles degrade much faster than the mean past 60%. It applies more forcefully to disks than to CPUs because a disk is a queueing system whose requests typically cannot be interrupted and must wait their turn, whereas on a CPU higher-priority work can preempt. Add that the 55% is itself a five-minute average, which hides shorter periods at much higher utilization. (c) Ask for the full distribution and a shorter interval rather than three summary numbers — and specifically for saturation (queue length) alongside utilization. The visualization is a heat map: it quantises both axes into buckets and colours by event count, which solves the two problems of a scatter plot at this scale — the visual density limit, where dense points merge into a wall of paint, and the volume of data that must be collected and processed for every event. It shows one system or thousands the same way, makes a bimodal distribution immediately legible, and leaves high-latency outliers visible as isolated blocks high in the map.

questions.where: Part 4 · Question 2 — the campaign and the scaling claim
questions.prompt: A service handles 2,000 requests/s. It runs on 24 CPUs averaging 45% utilization, and CPU is the busiest resource. Marketing expects a campaign to triple traffic. An architect proposes doubling the instance count and, separately, claims the system “scales linearly, so twice the machines means twice the throughput”. A previous scaling test showed throughput rising to a peak at eight instances and then falling as more were added. (a) Compute the request rate at which CPU saturates, showing the arithmetic, and state two reasons the figure is optimistic. (b) Name the scalability profile the previous test shows, say which of the two models is needed to describe it and why, and say what that implies for the doubling proposal. (c) Say what you would measure before the campaign and name the method that would let you compose the cheapest configuration that meets the requirement.
questions.ideal: (a) CPU per request = total CPU% ÷ requests = 24 × 45% ÷ 2,000 = 1,080 ÷ 2,000 = 0.54% CPU per request. Maximum requests/s = 100% × 24 CPUs ÷ 0.54 = 2,400 ÷ 0.54 ≈ 4,440 requests/s. Two reasons it is optimistic: it is a rough best-case estimate — some other limiting factor may be encountered before requests reach that rate — and it rests on a single data point, one throughput figure against one utilization figure, where monitoring over time would give several pairs and a much better extrapolation. Also creditable: long before 100% the queueing effects of the previous question apply; and a tripling of traffic to 6,000 requests/s exceeds the estimate by a wide margin anyway. (b) Throughput rising to a peak and then falling as instances are added is the coherence profile — the tax of maintaining coherency, including propagating changes, has begun to outweigh the benefit of scaling. Amdahl's Law of Scalability models contention only, C(N) = N/(1 + α(N−1)), which flattens but does not decline; you need the Universal Scalability Law, C(N) = N/(1 + α(N−1) + βN(N−1)), whose β term is coherency delay — and note that with β = 0 the USL becomes Amdahl. The implication for the proposal is direct and uncomfortable: the system does not scale linearly, and past the peak adding instances reduces throughput, so doubling the count may deliver less capacity than they have now, not twice as much. (c) Measure across a range of N — by observation over time or experimentally with micro-benchmarking or a load generator — and fit the model by regression to obtain α and β, then plot the data against the model, because a deviation is itself informative: either the model is wrong or your understanding of the system's real scalability is. Also collect multiple throughput-and-utilization pairs to firm up the resource-limit extrapolation. The method for composing the cheapest configuration that still meets the requirement is factor analysis: test at maximum, change one factor at a time and attribute a percentage drop and a cost saving to each, then choose the combination that meets the target — eight binary factors need about ten tests rather than 256 — and retest the chosen configuration, since components can behave differently together than their individual measurements predict.

questions.prompt: Give both definitions of utilization, the example that separates them, and say which metric decides whether a busy resource is actually a bottleneck.
questions.ideal: Time-based utilization is U = B/T: the average amount of time the resource was busy, as a proportion of the observation period. It is the definition from queueing theory and the one operating system tools report — a disk tool calls it percent busy, which conveys the underlying measurement better. Capacity-based utilization is the proportion of the throughput the resource is able to deliver that it is currently delivering; at 100% of that it cannot accept any more work. The example that separates them is a lift, which may be considered utilized whenever it is moving between floors and can still accept more passengers while busy 100% of the time; the same is true of a disk buffering writes in its on-disk cache, and of a storage array running at 100% because some disk is always busy while many sit idle. 100% busy does not mean 100% capacity. The metric that decides whether a busy resource is actually a bottleneck is saturation — the degree to which it has queued work it cannot service, measured as a wait-queue length or as time spent waiting. Any non-zero saturation is a performance issue, because it is time spent waiting, which is latency.

questions.prompt: Explain why converting a performance metric to latency is worth doing, and name two things it makes possible that a rate metric does not.
questions.ideal: Because latency is a time, and time is the one unit that is comparable across components. Two things it makes possible that a rate metric does not: performance issues can be quantified and then ranked against each other, because they are expressed in the same units; and a predicted speedup can be calculated by considering how much latency would be reduced or removed. Neither can be accurately performed using something like IOPS. The illustration: choosing between 100 network I/O and 50 disk I/O is a complicated question involving network hops, drop and retransmit rates, I/O size, random versus sequential access and disk type — but comparing 100 ms of total network I/O against 50 ms of total disk I/O makes the difference obvious. One caution when quantifying a gain this way: make sure the latency is measured as a synchronous component of the request, because asynchronous work such as a background write flush does not directly affect the application's response.

questions.prompt: Name the three anti-methods, give the feature they all share, say why the ad hoc checklist is not one of them, and say what you should ask someone who has redirected an issue to another team.
questions.ideal: The streetlight anti-method: the absence of a deliberate methodology — choosing observability tools that are familiar, found on the internet, or picked at random, to see whether anything obvious shows up; named for the drunk searching under the streetlight, not because he lost his keys there but because that is where the light is best. The random change anti-method: an experimental one, in which you guess where the problem may be and change things until the symptom goes away — pick something, change it one way, measure, change it the other way, measure, keep whatever beat the baseline, repeat. The blame-someone-else anti-method: find a component you are not responsible for, hypothesise that the issue is with it, redirect it to the team responsible, and when proven wrong go back to step one. The feature they share is a lack of data leading to the hypothesis — stated explicitly as the way to identify blame-someone-else, and equally true of the other two; in the streetlight case there is no theory at all, only a step taken with nothing observed behind it. The ad hoc checklist method is not among them because it is a genuine method: stepping through a canned list of checks provides the most value in the shortest time frame and is an effective way to make sure a whole team can check for common issues. Its weaknesses are different in kind — every entry is a point-in-time recommendation that must be constantly updated, and checklists tend to focus on issues with known fixes that are easy to document, such as tunable settings, rather than custom fixes to source code or the environment. What to ask someone who has redirected an issue: for the screenshots showing which tools were run and how the output was interpreted, which you can then take to someone else for a second opinion.

questions.prompt: Give the six problem-statement questions and say why this method should come before any tool.
questions.ideal: What makes you think there is a performance problem? Has this system ever performed well? What changed recently — software, hardware, load? Can the problem be expressed in terms of latency or runtime? Does the problem affect other people or applications, or is it just you? What is the environment — which software and hardware are used, which versions, what configuration? It should come before any tool because simply asking and answering these questions often points to an immediate cause and solution: performance issues have been resolved by this method alone, over the phone, without logging in to any server or looking at any metric. It costs no tooling, no access and no measurement, so there is nothing to trade against doing it first.

questions.prompt: State the USE method, give its three metrics in the order they should be checked with the reason for that order, and say what it does differently from the tools method.
questions.ideal: The USE method: for every resource, check utilization, saturation and errors. Resources means all the physical functional components of the server — processors, memory, network interfaces, storage devices, controllers, interconnects and buses — and software resources too where the metrics make sense. Utilization is checked as a percentage over an interval, saturation as a wait-queue length, errors as a count. The order is errors first, then saturation, then utilization. Errors come first because they are usually objective rather than subjective metrics and so are quick to interpret, making it time-efficient to rule them out before investigating the others. Saturation comes second because it is quicker to interpret than utilization: any level of saturation can be an issue. Utilization is left until last because it needs the most interpretation. What it does differently from the tools method: it iterates over resources rather than tools. You create a complete list of questions first, and only then search for tools to answer them — so a question no available tool can answer becomes a recorded known-unknown, which is extremely useful information, instead of an invisible gap. The tools method instead gives an incomplete view bounded by the tools you have, and its user is unaware the view is incomplete and may remain unaware.

questions.prompt: State the RED method and explain precisely how the request rate distinguishes a load problem from an architecture problem.
questions.ideal: The RED method: for every service, check the request rate, the errors and the duration. Request rate is the number of service requests per second, errors is the number of requests that failed, and duration is the time for requests to complete — for which distribution statistics such as percentiles should be considered in addition to the average. The task is to draw a diagram of the service architecture and make sure all three are monitored for each service. The request rate provides an important early clue about load versus architecture: if the request rate has been steady but the request duration has increased, that points to a problem with the architecture, meaning the service itself; if both the request rate and the duration have increased, then the problem may be one of the load applied, which can then be investigated further using workload characterization. The two methods are complementary — USE for machine health, RED for user health.

questions.prompt: Give workload characterization's four questions, and say why they should be asked even when you are confident of the answers.
questions.ideal: Who is causing the load — process ID, user ID, remote address? Why is the load being called — code path, stack trace? What are the load characteristics — IOPS, throughput, direction such as read or write, and type, including variance such as standard deviation where appropriate? How is the load changing over time — is there a daily pattern? They should be asked even when you have strong expectations about the answers because you may be surprised. The worked example is a database whose clients are configured to be a pool of web servers: checking the addresses anyway reveals that the entire internet appears to be sending load, which is a denial-of-service attack. The wider point is that the best performance wins come from eliminating unnecessary work, which may be caused by a malfunctioning application, a bad configuration such as backups running during peak hours, or an attack — and characterizing the workload is what identifies these. Where the identified workload cannot be eliminated, resource controls can be used to throttle it instead.

questions.prompt: Name the method that runs with no load applied, give its four questions, and say why it is the one people skip.
questions.ideal: Static performance tuning. It focuses on issues of the configured architecture rather than the dynamic performance of an applied load, and can be performed when the system is at rest with no load applied. Its four questions, stepped through for every component of the system: does the component make sense — is it outdated or underpowered? Does the configuration make sense for the intended workload? Was the component auto-configured into the best state for the intended workload? And has the component experienced an error such that it is now in a degraded state? Examples of what it finds: a network interface negotiated to a tenth of its speed, a failed disk in a redundant pool, an old version of the operating system or firmware, a file system nearly full, a record size mismatched to the workload's I/O size, an application left running in a costly debug mode, a server accidentally configured as a network router, or a server reaching to a remote data centre for something available locally. It is the one people skip because these issues are easy to check for — the hard part is remembering to do it.

questions.prompt: Give both scalability formulas, say what each parameter represents, and state what has happened to mean response time beyond 60% utilization under M/D/1 — and why that matters more for disks than for CPUs.
questions.ideal: Amdahl's Law of Scalability: C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1)), where C(N) is the relative capacity, N is the scaling dimension such as CPU count or user load, and α, between 0 and 1, is the degree of seriality — how far the system deviates from linear scalability. It corresponds to the contention profile. The Universal Scalability Law: C(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1)), where β is the coherency parameter, covering the cost of maintaining data coherency including propagating changes; it corresponds to the coherence profile and includes the effects of contention, and when β equals zero it becomes Amdahl's Law. Under M/D/1, beyond 60% utilization the average response time has doubled, and by 80% it has tripled — from r = s(2 − ρ)/2(1 − ρ). Disks feel this far more sharply than CPUs: a disk behaves as a queueing system in which an in-flight request generally cannot be set aside, so everything behind it waits its turn — which is the reason disk utilization starts hurting a long way short of 100%. A CPU escapes that, since work of higher priority can displace what is running. Note too that M/D/1 flatters the situation: where service times vary rather than being fixed, the average climbs further still, and past 60% the upper percentiles fall away considerably more steeply than the average does.

questions.prompt: Explain why a mean can be worse than useless for a bimodal distribution, name two other statistics that also fail there, and give the only reliable alternative.
questions.ideal: Because means, standard deviations and percentiles are intended for normal-like or unimodal distributions, and system performance is often bimodal — low latencies for a fast code path and high ones for a slow one, or low for cache hits and high for cache misses, with sometimes more than two modes. The worked example is disk I/O latency for a mixed workload with a mode below 1 ms for on-disk cache hits and a mode peaking around 7 ms for misses; the mean is 3.3 ms, which is not the index of central tendency but almost the opposite, and is seriously misleading as a metric because it falls between the two things the system actually does. Two other statistics that also fail there: the standard deviation and percentiles, both of which assume a well-behaved distribution — and the median, while useful against outliers, likewise summarises rather than reveals the shape. The only reliable alternative is to inspect the full distribution, for example with a histogram, and visualizations such as a scatter plot or, at scale, a heat map, which quantises both axes into buckets and so shows the structure of one system or thousands the same way. Every time you see an average used as a performance metric, especially an average latency, ask what the distribution is.

The random change anti-method: guessing where the problem may be and changing things until the symptom goes away, keeping whatever beat the baseline. The blame-someone-else anti-method: finding a component you are not responsible for, hypothesising it is the cause, redirecting the issue to that team, and repeating when proven wrong. And the ad hoc checklist method, which is genuinely valuable but consists of point-in-time recommendations that decay and skews toward issues with easily documented fixes. The feature they share is that the hypothesis arrives before the data, or with no data behind it at all — a lack of data leading to the hypothesis is stated as the way to identify blame-someone-else specifically. What to ask someone who has redirected an issue: for the screenshots showing which tools were run and how the output was interpreted, which you can then take to someone else for a second opinion.
retired.retired_because: the question asked for "four anti-methods"; the source names three, and the ad hoc checklist is a method rather than an anti-method

competencies.title: Benchmarking — What the Number Is, How It Lies, Which Kind, and Active Analysis

questions.prompt: A team is choosing between two managed database offerings. An engineer runs a load tool against both for ten minutes each, produces a slide showing one is 1.8× faster, and circulates it. Asked what limited each run, they say the tool reported no errors and both machines “looked busy”. The slide is scheduled for a purchasing decision on Friday. The team's performance specialist is offered a slot on Thursday to “review the numbers”. (a) Name the four things that must be understood about any benchmark result, and say which of them this exercise has established. (b) Explain why the Thursday review slot is the wrong intervention, in terms of what evidence still exists by then. (c) Name the additional quantity that this particular purpose requires, say how it is defined, and give two further questions you would put to the engineer before Friday.
questions.ideal: (a) The four are: what is being tested; what the limiting factor or factors are; any perturbations that might affect the results; and what conclusions may be drawn. This exercise has established none of them. The tool's name is standing in for the first, “looked busy” is not a limiting factor — the resource sweep offers only two outcomes, something at 100% or a system not driven to its limit, and neither has been shown — nothing was checked for perturbations, and the conclusion (1.8×) has been drawn without any of the three that would license it. “No errors reported” is worth something but is not one of the four. (b) Because three of the four questions can only be answered from the system while the load is applied, and by Thursday the machines are idle. This is the staffing mistake in its usual form: junior staff execute the benchmarks and performance experts are brought in to explain the results afterwards. The correction is scheduling rather than skill — engage the expert during the run, so they can analyse the live system with drill-down to quantify the limiter. If Thursday is genuinely all there is, the useful output is a list of the assumptions nobody had time to check, published with the result as a to-do list for verification. (c) The purpose here is a purchase, so the required extra quantity is the price/performance ratio, where price can be quantified as the five-year capital cost of the equipment. Further questions worth putting: what was the limiting factor in each run; what was the configuration of each system, and does either resemble what we would actually buy and run; was the workload representative of ours, and how was that established; how long did each run last and how many times was it repeated; what were the success and failure counts; is this an average or a peak, and what is the distribution.

questions.prompt: Two results land on your desk on the same morning. The first says: “Storage cluster: 1.4 million operations per second.” The second reports a four-hour soak test of an internal message bus. It states the payload size and the batch size, gives the sustained rate and the total volume moved, notes that the producer host's network interface sat at 96% of line rate for the whole run while the consumer host's processors never went above 40%, breaks the producer's processor time down across serialisation, compression, the network stack and the application's own bookkeeping with no single part dominant, and then stops. (a) Say what the second result does that the first does not, mapping each of its elements to one of the four questions. (b) Explain why the observation about the producer's network interface changes what the sustained-rate figure is a claim about. (c) The first result's author says the second is “overkill for a headline number”. Give the strongest version of their case, then say what you would still require before quoting the 1.4 million figure anywhere.
questions.ideal: (a) The second result answers the four questions and the first answers none. What is being tested: the second states the payload size, the batch size and the volume moved, precisely enough to reproduce; the first says only “operations”, which could be anything of any size. What the limiting factor is: the second names it — the producer's network interface at 96% of line rate throughout, with the consumer's processors never above 40%, so one component was at its limit and the other plainly was not; the first offers nothing. Perturbations: the second's decomposition of producer processor time across four named areas, none dominant, shows nothing unexpected was consuming the machine during the run; the first gives no basis on which to check. What may be concluded: the second stops at what the measurement supports and draws no wider claim; the first's single number is already a claim about a whole cluster. (b) Because a network interface at 96% of line rate makes the sustained rate a statement about that link, not about the message bus. The same software on the same hosts behind a faster interface would give a different figure, so the number cannot be quoted as a property of the bus, of the consumer, or of the pair — and for the bus it is a floor rather than a ceiling. Naming the limiter is what converts a measurement into a claim with a subject. (c) The strongest version of their case: a headline figure exists to be compared with other headline figures, decomposition costs analyst time that a purchasing conversation will not read, and if the cluster genuinely served 1.4 million operations then it did so regardless of where the processor time went. What you would still require before quoting it: what the operations actually were and at what size; what limited the run, established by observing the system rather than asserted; whether any component reached 100%, since if none did the figure is a floor rather than a ceiling; the error and timeout counts; the duration and the number of repeats with their variation; and the configuration, so the reader knows which machine the number is about. Absent those, the honest form is the number plus an explicit list of the assumptions nobody checked.

questions.prompt: A team evaluates two message brokers. The load tool is run for 20 seconds against each; broker A reports 3× the throughput of broker B and is chosen. Later, in production, A is slower. Investigation finds four things: the tool ran as a single process on one client machine; broker B had been configured to acknowledge writes durably while A had not; roughly 8% of B's requests had returned errors that the tool counted as completed operations; and the nightly index rebuild had been running on the B host for the last six seconds of its run. The engineer's summary slide had said only “A: 240k msg/s, B: 80k msg/s”. (a) Name each of the four named failures at work here, and say for each whether it made the measurement wrong or the claim wrong. (b) Two of these four have a stated remedy that costs almost nothing; give both remedies and the specific rule of thumb attached to one of them. (c) The slide itself commits a fifth failure independent of the four. Name it and state what the slide should have carried instead.
questions.ideal: (a) Four named failures. Complex benchmark tools, in its specific form benchmarking the benchmark: a single-process client means the reported result may be the tool's own ceiling rather than either broker's — measurement wrong. Changing multiple factors: one broker acknowledged writes durably and the other did not, so the two runs differ in more than the product — measurement wrong. Ignoring errors: roughly 8% of B's requests errored and were counted as completed operations, and errors perform differently from normal operations and skew the result — measurement wrong. Ignoring perturbations: an index rebuild ran on the B host through the last six seconds of a twenty-second run — measurement wrong. All four are in the accidental-measurement quadrant, which is where ten of the sixteen live. (b) Two near-free remedies. For perturbations: make the runs longer — minutes instead of seconds — with the rule that a benchmark's duration should not be shorter than one second, then run it several times and examine the standard deviation, which should be as small as possible. For errors: check the operation success/fail ratio before reading any throughput figure; the checklist puts this as “did it error?” and “did it even happen?”. (c) The slide commits numbers without analysis: bare results with no analytical detail, which can be a sign that the author is inexperienced and has assumed they are trustworthy and final. Every benchmark number should be accompanied by a description of the limit encountered and the analysis performed. Failing that, the slide should have carried the list of assumptions nobody had time to check — that the tool is not the bottleneck, that the two configurations are equivalent, that the operations succeeded, that nothing else was running — which then becomes the verification to-do list if the decision turns out to matter.

questions.prompt: Your company's product must win a customer evaluation consisting of four separate benchmarks; the customer will buy only if you win all four. Your engineers believe you are genuinely a coin-flip against the incumbent on each. Marketing proposes three responses: (i) commission an outside firm quickly and cheaply to produce a comparison against the incumbent; (ii) add a configuration switch that detects the evaluation's access pattern and pre-fetches for it; (iii) skip benchmarks entirely and sell on features. (a) Compute your probability of winning all four, and state the summarised rule this illustrates. (b) Take each of the three proposals in turn, name the failure it corresponds to, and give the specific reason it backfires — for (ii), say which body introduced a mechanism against it, what that mechanism is, and what price rule accompanies it. (c) Name the failure that proposal (iii) itself commits, and describe the one intervention that genuinely improves the odds.
questions.ideal: (a) 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.0625, so 6.25% — about one chance in sixteen. The rule is the benchmark paradox: “if your product's chances of winning a benchmark are 50/50, you'll usually lose”, because customers who want to be sure run several and expect you to win them all, and the more benchmarks the worse the chances. (b) Proposal (i) is benchmarking the competition, and in its cheap-third-party form it is also the misleading benchmarks variant where several firms are engaged not for expertise but for a fast inexpensive result and the best is kept. It backfires because customers use a product for months and tune it, while you have days — so you can only produce untuned and therefore unrealistic results, and the competitor's customers, who are the target of the exercise, will recognise them, costing your company credibility with exactly the people it was trying to impress. Proposal (ii) is a benchmark special: engineering the product to score on the benchmark while disregarding actual customer performance. The transaction-processing body — the one whose focus is price/performance — answered it with specification rather than argument, adding an anti-benchmark-special clause prohibiting all implementations that improve benchmark results but not real-world performance or pricing, and accompanying it with a price requirement that the total price be within 2% of what a customer would actually pay, which closes the parallel trick of quoting deep discounts nobody would receive. (c) Proposal (iii) commits the pitfall that ignoring benchmarks is itself a benchmarking failure. The intervention that genuinely improves the odds is to stop being a coin flip and to make sure your own results are the best your product can honestly produce — the friendly-fire remedy: test the top-performing system and configuration, drive it to its true limit and be able to say what the bottleneck was, benchmark the current version on the best available equipment, and share the results with engineering before publication so they can spot what was misconfigured or left off.

questions.prompt: A team is replacing an object storage tier. The new tier has slower spinning media but four times the memory for metadata and small-object caching. They plan to capture a week of production traffic at the block device layer and replay it against the new tier, on the grounds that this is “as close to production as we can get without risking production”. A colleague suggests instead measuring the production request mix and driving a synthetic workload from it, and separately running a small set of narrow tests. (a) Predict the result of the replay plan and explain the mechanism, naming the level at which the trace was captured and why that matters here. (b) Name the general property of replay that makes it disappointing even when the capture level is right. (c) For the colleague's narrow tests, specify the two multiplying factors that must be applied to each test, and say what setting of each you would use to answer the question “does the extra memory help?”
questions.ideal: (a) It will show a regression, and the regression will be an artefact. The trace was captured at the block device layer, which means it records the requests the old system's cache failed to absorb. Replaying those against the new tier asks its slower spinning media to service, from disk, precisely the traffic the new tier's four-times-larger cache was bought to absorb — so the new tier is measured on its weakest component with its strongest one bypassed. The real production workload would have improved, returning largely from cache, which replaying device-level events cannot simulate. It is the storage-upgrade case exactly: 10K rpm disks replaced by 7,200 rpm disks with sixteen times the file system cache, a replay that showed a regression, and a lost sale; it is a case of testing the wrong thing. (b) Even at the right level, a replay disappoints because a recording cannot react: when the server's characteristics and delivered latency change, the captured client workload is unlikely to respond naturally to those differences, which may prove no better than a simulated workload — and when too much faith is placed in it, things can get worse. Subtle timing effects can also disturb it. (c) Every micro-benchmark test is multiplied by working set size and thread count. Working set much smaller than main memory caches entirely, so the file system software is what you investigate; much larger than main memory minimises cache and drives the test toward disk I/O. Thread count, assuming a small working set: single-threaded tests file system performance at the current CPU clock speed; enough threads to saturate all CPUs tests the maximum of system, file system and CPUs together. To answer “does the extra memory help?” you need both settings of the working set on both tiers, and in particular a working set sized to fit the new tier's memory but not the old tier's — that is the cell where the extra cache is the only thing that differs. Run single-threaded to attribute the result to the software path and saturating to establish the ceiling.

questions.prompt: Your team maintains an internal benchmark written six years ago to imitate the then-current API traffic of your service. Traffic has since shifted heavily toward a batch endpoint that did not exist when the benchmark was written. A proposal to rewrite it is resisted: two years of published quarterly results use the current version, and rewriting would break the trend line. Separately, a vendor offers you results from an independent body's suite instead. (a) Name the kind of benchmark your internal one is, and the specific weakness of that kind that this situation is an instance of. (b) State plainly what is being traded against what in the resistance to rewriting, and say what you would do with the two years of results either way. (c) Give three things an independent body's result offers that your internal benchmark does not, and the one question you must answer before the vendor's result is usable at all — including the method that answers it.
questions.ideal: (a) It is a simulation, also called a macro-benchmark: a benchmark imitating a customer application workload, normally built from workload characterization of the production environment. The weakness this is an instance of is that customer usage patterns change over time, so simulations require updating and adjusting to stay relevant — and there is resistance to that when published results based on the older version would no longer be usable for comparison with the new one. (b) What is being traded is comparability against relevance: two years of quarterly results form a series that only holds together while the benchmark is unchanged, and the benchmark is only worth running while it resembles the traffic. Either way, keep the two years and relabel them as measurements of the old workload — they remain valid for comparison with each other and invalid as statements about current performance. Do not plot old and new on one line; start a new series and say plainly which property you chose. (c) An independent body's suite offers: tests that are well defined and documented and must be executed under guidelines so results are as intended; full disclosure of the configured environment, which may be audited, and depending on the body either price/performance or a component and tuning list; and results that already exist for a variety of vendors and products, so you can compare without running anything. The question you must answer first is whether it resembles your production workload — for a current workload that is decided by workload characterization, measuring the real makeup of your traffic and comparing it against what the suite exercises.

questions.prompt: A colleague reports that a new caching layer sustains 400,000 reads per second of 4 Kbyte objects, measured from a bank of client machines across a single 10 Gbit/s network interface into the cache server. They add that the run lasted 30 seconds, the client CPUs were at 40%, the server CPUs were at 55%, and no component reached saturation. They would like to publish the figure. (a) Perform the check that this result invites, showing the arithmetic, and state your conclusion. (b) Give the most likely explanation for a result of this shape, and name the check that would have caught it during the run. (c) Independently of the arithmetic, the sentence “no component reached saturation” is itself a finding. Say what it establishes about the figure, using the disjunction that the resource sweep provides, and give the checklist question that puts the same point in three words.
questions.ideal: (a) The sanity check: 400,000 operations per second × 4 Kbytes = 1,600,000 Kbytes/s, which is about 1.6 Gbytes/s, or roughly 12.8 Gbit/s — before protocol headers — over a single 10 Gbit/s interface. That exceeds the known limit of the link, so the result is not merely doubtful, it is impossible, and the conclusion is that the figure is bogus. No further debate is needed; the arithmetic settles it. (b) The likely explanation is that the benchmark tested client caching and never drove the entire workload to the server, which is what results of this shape usually mean.
