During the run this would have been caught by observing the server — counting the operations actually arriving there and comparing them with what the clients reported — which is active benchmarking rather than reading the client's summary. (c) “No component reached saturation” is a finding in its own right, because the resource sweep offers exactly two outcomes: either some hardware or software component has reached 100% utilization, or you are not driving the system to its limit. Since nothing did, the second holds, so the figure is a floor rather than a ceiling and no limiting factor has been established — meaning the result cannot honestly be quoted at all. The checklist puts the same point in three words: “Why not double?”

questions.prompt: You have four hours of exclusive access to a shared, heavily contended reference system next month; five other teams want the same slot. Your task is to establish whether a proposed configuration change improves throughput, and to produce a figure that survives scrutiny. You are told the change “should be about 15% — run it before and after and take the difference”. (a) Name the analysis approach this access pattern forces you into, give its three phases, and say precisely what it can and cannot establish. (b) Explain why a single before-and-after pair is insufficient for a change of this size, naming the two properties you must understand to make sense of a pair of results. (c) Describe what you would do during the four hours, beyond running the two configurations, and why that work has to happen then rather than afterwards. (d) Give three of the six checklist questions you would answer before circulating any figure, and what each one would take.
questions.ideal: (a) Statistical analysis, which is the approach used where access to a large-scale system is both time-limited and expensive and many teams — sales, marketing, support, engineering, quality — want the same machine. Its three phases: selection of the benchmark tool, its configuration and the system performance metrics to capture; execution of the benchmark, collecting a large dataset of results and metrics; and interpretation of the data with statistical analysis, producing a report. It can establish consistency, variation, error margins and full distributions. It cannot establish what was actually measured — that evidence exists only while the load is applied, which is active benchmarking's job. (b) Because when benchmarking for code changes or non-regression testing it is crucial to understand the variation and the error margins in order to make sense of a pair of results. A claimed 15% difference means nothing if run-to-run variation is of the same order, and a single before-and-after pair contains no information about that variation at all. (c) During the four hours, beyond running the two configurations: analyse the system while the load is applied — confirm the benchmark is testing what it claims, sweep resources for utilization, saturation and errors until either something is at 100% or you accept the system was not driven to its limit, and profile both target and benchmark software to see whether anything unexpected is limiting it. Also collect as much performance data as the collection overhead allows, including variation, full distributions and error margins, so forensic analysis is possible afterwards; a script that dumps every available counter before, during and after each run is the standard form. It has to happen then because the machine is not yours next month, because the metrics are expensive enough that a problem found later means redoing them, and because what was measured is unrecoverable once the load stops. (d) Three of the six, with what each requires: Why not double? — needs the limiter, established by the resource sweep and profiling during the run. Does it reproduce? — needs repeated runs and their standard deviation, which is also what makes the pair of results interpretable. Did it error? — needs the operation success/fail ratio, since errors perform differently from normal operations and a high error rate skews the result. (Equally acceptable: did it break limits?, needing the arithmetic against known component limits; does it matter?, needing workload characterization of production; did it even happen?, needing confirmation at the target that the work arrived.)

questions.prompt: State what a benchmark result is a fact about and what it is not, give the six qualities of a good benchmark and the additional quantity needed before a purchase, and say how that quantity's price component is defined.
questions.ideal: A benchmark result is a fact about how fast this system ran this particular benchmark, under these particular conditions. It is not a fact about your system or a prediction of your production performance: a benchmark reports only the speed at which the system executed it, and the work of interpreting that and of judging how far it carries over to your own environment is left entirely to you. The six qualities of a good benchmark are that it is repeatable, so comparisons are possible; observable, so performance can be analysed and understood; portable, so it can be run on competitors and across releases; easily presented, so everyone understands the results; realistic, so measurements reflect what customers experience; and runnable, so developers can test changes quickly. Where systems are being compared with an intent to purchase, a seventh is required — the price/performance ratio — with price quantified as the equipment's capital cost across five years. Observable is worth singling out, because a benchmark that cannot be watched while it runs cannot be analysed at all.

questions.prompt: Give the four things that must be understood about any benchmark result, say how they are best served, and explain what specifically is lost by bringing in a performance expert after the run has completed.
questions.ideal: What the test actually exercises; which factor or factors are limiting it; which perturbations could be disturbing the figure; and which conclusions the measurement will support. Answering them calls for deep familiarity with three things at once: the behaviour of the benchmark software, the way the system responds to it, and the relationship between the figure and the environment it is meant to describe. Given the benchmark tool and access to the system, they are best answered by analysing the system's performance during the run itself, drilling down far enough to explain and put numbers on whatever is limiting it. Bringing the expert in afterwards is a common mistake in which junior staff execute the benchmarks and performance experts are asked to explain the results once the run has completed. What is lost is the evidence itself: once the machine is idle there is nothing left to observe, so most of what would answer three of the four questions is gone with it, and the fourth — what may be concluded — is only safe once the first three are. The correction is one of scheduling rather than skill: engage the expert during the run. Where there is no access at all, two further questions arise: what the system environment was and how it was configured.

questions.prompt: State the casual benchmarking formula in its A/B/C form, give the standard example with the reason the discrepancy is so large, and say why a correctly functioning tool does not save you from it.
questions.ideal: Casual benchmarking is the fire-and-forget approach, and the formula is: you benchmark A, but actually measure B, and conclude you have measured C. The standard example is the many tools that claim or imply they report the performance of disks, when what they exercise is the file system. The discrepancy can be orders of magnitude, because file systems employ caching and buffering to substitute disk I/O with memory I/O, so the number you get describes memory speed rather than device speed. A correctly functioning tool does not save you, because the tool may be behaving exactly as designed and testing the file system faithfully while your conclusions about the disks are still wildly incorrect — the defect is in the inference, not in the software. Doing benchmarking well requires rigour to check what is actually measured, and an understanding of what was tested in order to form valid conclusions. This is particularly hard for a beginner, who has no instinct for whether a number is suspicious: a thermometer reading a thousand degrees would be obviously wrong, but benchmark numbers are unfamiliar and carry no such signal.

questions.prompt: Explain what should accompany every benchmark number, what to publish instead when there is no time for analysis, and give the summarised rule about how long a result deserves before you trust it.
questions.ideal: Any benchmark figure ought to travel with two companions: a statement of the limit that was reached, and an account of the analysis done to establish it. Bare results provided with no analytical detail can be a sign that the author is inexperienced and has assumed the results are trustworthy and final, when this is usually just the beginning of an investigation — an investigation that often finds the results were wrong or confusing. Where there is genuinely no time for careful analysis, the thing to publish instead is a list of the assumptions you have not had time to check, included with the results: that the benchmark tool is not buggy, that the disk I/O test actually measures disk I/O, that the tool drove disk I/O to its limit as intended, and that this type of I/O is relevant for this application. That list then becomes a to-do list for further verification if the result is later deemed important enough to spend more effort on. The summarised rule is that if you have spent less than a week studying a benchmark result, it is probably wrong.

questions.prompt: Distinguish ignoring variance from ignoring perturbations: define each, give an example, and give the specific remedy for each — including the minimum run duration and the statistic to check across repeats.
questions.ideal: Ignoring variance is a failure to reproduce the variation in the workload you are simulating. Benchmark tools, especially micro-benchmarks, often apply a steady and consistent workload based on the average of a series of measurements of real-world characteristics. The example is a disk workload found to average 500 reads and 50 writes per second, which a tool then simulates either at those rates or at the 10:1 ratio so that higher rates can be tested. That erases the fact that the rate and the mix vary and that some types occur orthogonally: writes may arrive in bursts every 10 seconds from asynchronous write-back flushing while synchronous reads are steady, and those bursts can cause real production issues, such as queueing the reads, that a steady average never reproduces. One possible remedy is for the benchmark to use a Markov model, reflecting the probability that a write will be followed by another write. Ignoring perturbations is a failure to consider external activity affecting the results: a timed system activity such as a backup executing during the run, monitoring agents collecting statistics once per minute, or, in the cloud, unseen tenants on the same host system. The remedy is to make runs longer — minutes instead of seconds — with the rule that the duration of a benchmark should not be shorter than one second, since short tests can be unusually perturbed by device interrupts pinning the thread during interrupt service routines, by scheduling decisions in the kernel that delay migrating queued threads in order to preserve CPU affinity, and by the warmth of the CPU caches. Repeat the test several times and inspect the standard deviation across the repeats, aiming for it to be as small as it can be; also collect the distribution of operation latency, not just the total runtime, so outliers can be seen and their details recorded.

questions.prompt: State the benchmark paradox and its arithmetic, then explain why benchmarking a competitor is self-defeating and what would have to be done to do it honestly.
questions.ideal: The benchmark paradox is that where a product has an even chance of winning any one benchmark, it will usually lose overall. The arithmetic is that customers buying on performance often want to be really sure, which means running not one benchmark but several and wanting the product to win them all; at a 50% probability each, the probability of winning three is 0.5 times 0.5 times 0.5, which is 0.125, or 12.5%. The more benchmarks, with the requirement of winning them all, the worse the chances — and ignoring benchmarks in response is itself a benchmarking pitfall. Benchmarking a competitor is self-defeating because customers do not evaluate a product for five minutes — they live with it for months, analysing and tuning as they go and shaking out the worst issues within the first few weeks. You do not have weeks to spend analysing and tuning a competitor, so in the time available you can only gather untuned and therefore unrealistic results — and your competitor's customers, who are the target of the marketing activity, may well recognise untuned results when they are posted, and the effect is that your company forfeits credibility with precisely the audience the exercise was meant to win over. To do it honestly you would have to spend serious time tuning their product: analysing its performance with the usual techniques, searching out best practices, customer forums and bug databases, possibly bringing in outside expertise, and then making the same effort for your own product before finally running the head-to-head benchmarks.

questions.prompt: Define a benchmark special, say when the term came into use and over what, and give the two specification changes the industry body introduced in response.
questions.ideal: A benchmark special is when a vendor studies a popular or industry benchmark and then engineers the product so that it scores well on that benchmark, while disregarding actual customer performance; it is also called optimising for the benchmark. The term came into use in 1993, with the TPC-A benchmark: a consulting firm charged that a database vendor had added a special option, discrete transactions, to its software for the sole purpose of inflating its results, and claimed this violated the spirit of the TPC because it was something a typical customer would not use. The vendor rejected the accusation, arguing with some justification that it had followed the letter of the law in the benchmark specifications, and that since benchmark specials were not addressed there it was unfair to accuse them of violating anything. The two changes introduced in response were an anti-benchmark-special clause, prohibiting every such implementation that lifts benchmark scores without lifting real-world performance or pricing; and, because the focus is price/performance and the parallel trick is to base results on deep discounts no customer would actually get, a price requirement that the total price must be within 2% of the price a customer would pay for the configuration. These were addressed many years ago, and you should not necessarily expect benchmark specials today.

questions.prompt: Describe the design of a micro-benchmark set: the five sample file system tests with the intent of each, and the two factors every test is multiplied by, with what each setting of each factor tests.
questions.ideal: Designing a file system micro-benchmark means choosing the attributes to test — sequential or random I/O, I/O size, and direction — and then multiplying them out. The five sample tests and their intents are: sequential 512-byte reads, to test maximum realistic IOPS, using more and smaller I/O; sequential 1-Mbyte reads, to test maximum read throughput, using fewer and larger I/O so less time is spent on I/O initialization; sequential 1-Mbyte writes, to test maximum write throughput; random 512-byte reads, to test the effect of random I/O; and random 512-byte writes, to test the effect of rewrites. All of these are then multiplied by two additional factors. The first is working set size, the size of the data being accessed: much smaller than main memory, so that the data caches entirely in the file system cache and the performance of the file system software can be investigated; or much larger than main memory, to minimise the effect of the file system cache and drive the benchmark toward testing disk I/O. The second is thread count, assuming a small working set size: single-threaded, to test file system performance based on the current CPU clock speed; or multithreaded sufficiently to saturate all CPUs, to test the maximum performance of the system, the file system and the CPUs. These multiply quickly into a large matrix of tests, and statistical analysis techniques can be used to reduce the required set. Note also that focusing on top speeds is sunny day performance testing, and that cloudy or rainy day testing — contention, perturbations and workload variance — should be considered too.

questions.prompt: Compare simulation and replay: what each is, what each buys you, and what went wrong in the storage-upgrade case — naming the level of capture and the component whose improvement it hid.
questions.ideal: A simulation, sometimes called a macro-benchmark, imitates a customer application workload, and may be based on workload characterization of the production environment to determine the characteristics to simulate — for example a file-server workload composed of reads at 40%, writes at 7%, getattr at 19% and readdir at 1%. It buys you results that resemble how clients will perform with the real workload, if not closely then at least closely enough to be useful, and it can encompass many factors that would be time-consuming to investigate with micro-benchmarks and it can also capture interactions between parts of the system that are intricate enough for a narrow test to overlook entirely. It may be stateless, where each request is unrelated to the previous one and the type of each operation is chosen randomly according to measured probability, or stateful, where each request depends on client state and is better simulated with a Markov model. Its problems are that it can ignore variance, and that it ages as customer usage patterns change. A replay attempts to replay a trace log to the target, testing performance with the actual captured client operations, which sounds as good as testing in production. What it buys is real operations rather than a synthesised mix; the difficulty is that once the server's characteristics and the latency it delivers have changed, the recorded client traffic will not react to the difference the way a live client would, which can leave it no better than a synthesised workload — and worse, when too much faith is placed in it. In the storage-upgrade case, a customer's production workload was traced and replayed on new hardware, performance was worse and the sale was lost. The trace had been captured at the disk I/O level; the old system housed 10K rpm disks and the new one slower 7,200 rpm disks, but the new system also provided sixteen times the amount of file system cache along with faster processors. The component whose improvement the replay hid was therefore the file system cache: the actual production workload would have shown improved performance because it would have returned largely from cache, which replaying disk events did not simulate. It is a case of testing the wrong thing.

questions.prompt: Give the four steps of passive benchmarking and define active benchmarking, then describe the case study that showed a “hard drive” benchmark testing no disk at all — the sanity check that started it, the layers checked, and the conclusion.
questions.ideal: Passive benchmarking is the fire-and-forget strategy in which the benchmark is executed and then ignored until it has completed, the main objective being the collection of benchmark data; it is described as its own anti-methodology for comparison with active benchmarking. Its four steps are: pick a benchmark tool; run it with a variety of options; make a slide deck of the results; and hand the slides to management. Active benchmarking means analysing performance while the benchmark is running — not just after it is done — using observability tools, so that you can confirm the benchmark tests what it says it tests, understand what that is, and identify the true limiters of the system under test or of the benchmark itself. In the case study, a micro-benchmark suite whose documentation described it as a program to test hard drive performance reported 739 Kbytes per second on its first sequential-output per-character test. The sanity check was that if the test genuinely performed one I/O per character, the machine would have to be sustaining 739,000 I/O every second, which was implausible for disks. Checking disk statistics during the run showed no disk I/O reported at all. Tracing block events showed no block I/O issued and none completed, but buffers being dirtied. Cache statistics confirmed a workload of dirties — writes into the file system cache — with a 100% hit ratio and no misses. Counting calls at the virtual file system layer showed 1,176,936 writes against 13 reads, and a histogram of the size argument put 668,839 of those writes at one byte each. The conclusion was that the first test performs single-byte writes to the file system, which are absorbed by the file system cache, so it exercises no disk I/O at all despite what the tool's description implies; the option advertised as disabling write buffering did not in fact synchronise after each write, and the direct-I/O option failed outright, so there was no way to perform a per-character disk write test at all.

retired.reason: Part (a)-(c) turned on the source's own worked example — the 1981 network-stack analysis, taught earlier in the same booklet — so the first part tested recognition rather than retrieval. Replaced with an invented soak-test report.
retired.prompt: Two results land on your desk on the same morning. The first says: “Storage cluster: 1.4 million operations per second.” The second describes a transfer of a fixed payload between two hosts, states the record and packet sizes, reports the elapsed time and derived throughput, notes that the sending host was CPU saturated while the receiver had roughly a third of its capacity idle, and breaks the system time down across five kernel components, none dominant. (a) Say what the second result does that the first does not, mapping each to one of the four questions. (b) Explain why the observation about the sending host changes what the throughput figure is a claim about. (c) The first result's author says the second is “overkill for a headline number”. Give the strongest version of their case, then say what you would still require before quoting the 1.4 million figure anywhere.
retired.ideal: (a) The second result answers the four questions and the first answers none. What is being tested: the second states the payload size, the record size and the packet size, precisely enough to reproduce; the first says only “operations”. What the limiting factor is: the second says the sending host was CPU saturated while the receiver had roughly a third idle; the first offers nothing. Perturbations: the second's decomposition of system time across five components, none dominant, shows that nothing unexpected was consuming the machine; the first gives no basis to check. What may be concluded: the second stops at what the measurement supports and draws no wider claim; the first's single number is already a claim about a cluster. (b) Because a saturated sender makes the throughput a statement about that machine's processor, not about the network or the receiving system. The same wire and the same receiver with a faster sender would give a different figure, so the number cannot be quoted as a property of the link or of the pair. Naming the limiter is what converts a measurement into a claim with a subject. (c) The strongest version of their case: a headline figure exists to be compared with other headline figures, decomposition costs analyst time that a purchasing conversation will not read, and if the cluster genuinely served 1.4 million operations then it did so regardless of where the kernel time went. What you would still require before quoting it: what the operations actually were and at what size; what limited the run, established by observing the system rather than asserted; whether any component was at 100%, since if none was the figure is a floor rather than a ceiling; the error and timeout counts; the duration and the number of repeats with their variation; and the configuration, so the reader knows what machine the number is about. Absent those, the honest form is the number plus an explicit list of the assumptions nobody checked.

retired.reason: The prompt asked what mechanism 'the industry-standard bodies' introduced against benchmark specials. Only the transaction-processing body did; the prompt asserted something false. Reissued asking which body.
retired.prompt: Your company's product must win a customer evaluation consisting of four separate benchmarks; the customer will buy only if you win all four. Your engineers believe you are genuinely a coin-flip against the incumbent on each. Marketing proposes three responses: (i) commission an outside firm quickly and cheaply to produce a comparison against the incumbent; (ii) add a configuration switch that detects the evaluation's access pattern and pre-fetches for it; (iii) skip benchmarks entirely and sell on features. (a) Compute your probability of winning all four, and state the summarised rule this illustrates. (b) Take each of the three proposals in turn, name the failure it corresponds to, and give the specific reason it backfires — for (ii), say what mechanism the industry-standard bodies introduced against it and what price rule accompanies it. (c) Name the failure that proposal (iii) itself commits, and describe the one intervention that genuinely improves the odds.
retired.ideal: (a) 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.0625, so 6.25% — about one chance in sixteen. The rule is the benchmark paradox: “if your product's chances of winning a benchmark are 50/50, you'll usually lose”, because customers who want to be sure run several and expect you to win them all, and the more benchmarks the worse the chances. (b) Proposal (i) is benchmarking the competition, and in its cheap-third-party form it is also the misleading benchmarks variant where several firms are engaged not for expertise but for a fast inexpensive result and the best is kept. It backfires because customers use a product for months and tune it, while you have days — so you can only produce untuned and therefore unrealistic results, and the competitor's customers, who are the target of the exercise, will recognise them, costing your company credibility with exactly the people it was trying to impress. Proposal (ii) is a benchmark special: engineering the product to score on the benchmark while disregarding actual customer performance. The industry bodies answered it with specification rather than argument — an anti-benchmark-special clause prohibiting all implementations that improve benchmark results but not real-world performance or pricing — and accompanied it with a price requirement that the total price be within 2% of what a customer would actually pay, closing the parallel trick of quoting deep discounts nobody would receive. (c) Proposal (iii) commits the pitfall that ignoring benchmarks is itself a benchmarking failure. The intervention that genuinely improves the odds is to stop being a coin flip and to make sure your own results are the best your product can honestly produce — the friendly-fire remedy: test the top-performing system and configuration, drive it to its true limit and be able to say what the bottleneck was, benchmark the current version on the best available equipment, and share the results with engineering before publication so they can spot what was misconfigured or left off.

competencies.title: Incident Response & Postmortems — Structure, Mitigation, Practice, Learning
parts: The structure, before you need it

questions.prompt: A payments API starts returning errors for a subset of merchants. The on-call engineer opens a ticket, starts investigating, and posts findings into the ticket as they go. Over the next ninety minutes four other engineers notice the ticket and begin investigating in parallel; two of them independently rule out the same subsystem. The support team, fielding merchant calls, is asking the on-call engineer for updates roughly every ten minutes. Nobody has used the word “incident”. The on-call engineer's view is that they will declare one “if it turns out to be serious”. (a) Name the two distinct jobs now in progress, define each, and say which one has no owner. (b) Give the four basic principles, and identify which of them this situation violates and how. (c) Take the on-call engineer's reasoning seriously and say precisely what is wrong with it, using the three specific benefits that declaring early is said to provide. (d) Write the three sentences you would say to fix this in the next sixty seconds.
questions.ideal: (a) Resolving the incident — mitigating the impact and/or restoring the service to its previous condition — and managing it: coordinating the efforts of the responding teams efficiently, and ensuring communication flows both between the responders and to those interested in the incident's progress. Five people are resolving. Nobody is managing, and that is the job with no owner. (b) The four principles are: maintain a clear line of command; designate clearly defined roles; keep a working record of debugging and mitigation as you go; and declare incidents early and often. All four are broken. There is no line of command, because nobody is leading and four people joined without being asked. There are no roles — in particular nobody is doing communications, which is why the support team is interrupting the one person best placed to fix it. The record is a ticket used as a notebook rather than a working document of theories and eliminated causes, which is how two engineers came to rule out the same subsystem independently; with five responders that document should exist. And no incident has been declared. (c) The reasoning treats declaring as an escalation whose cost must be justified by severity. It is the opposite: declaring is the act that supplies the tools — the command line, the roles, the shared channel and the record — so waiting does not defer a cost, it forfeits three specific benefits. Declaring early prevents miscommunication between the separate groups working the problem; makes root-cause identification and resolution occur sooner; and loops relevant teams in earlier, which makes external communication faster and smoother. Each of those is already being lost here. The principle is early and often, precisely because standing a response down is trivial and starting one ninety minutes late is not. (d) Something close to: “I'm declaring an incident, and I'm the Incident Commander.” “You're Operations Lead — you own the merchant errors, and everything you rule out goes in the shared doc.” “You're Communications Lead — support and the status page come to you, not to us; everyone else into the incident channel now.”

questions.prompt: Three hours into a regional outage, the incident channel has nineteen participants. The commander — the engineer who first noticed the problem — is simultaneously answering questions from a director, running two debugging threads, and writing an update for the status page. A colleague who has run many incidents joins and offers to help. Separately, two responders have each spent forty minutes eliminating the same suspected cause without knowing about each other. (a) Diagnose the commander's situation in terms of the default rule about undelegated roles, and say what specifically has gone wrong as a result. (b) Give both of the moves available to the commander now that an experienced colleague has arrived, and say what each costs. (c) Name the artefact that would have prevented the duplicated forty minutes, say at what team size it should have been started, and state exactly what it holds. (d) The channel is now too noisy to follow. Give the specific split to make, and say what stays in each place.
questions.ideal: (a) By default the commander assumes all roles that have not been delegated yet. Nothing has been delegated, so this person is simultaneously Incident Commander, Operations Lead and Communications Lead. The consequence is that the one job only they can do — coordinating — is the one being starved, because it has no deadline attached to it while the director and the status page do. The visible symptom is the duplicated forty minutes: coordination is what prevents two people doing the same elimination, and coordination is not happening. (b) Two moves are available, and both are normal. The commander may hand off the commander role to the experienced colleague and take the Operations Lead role themselves — cost: a handover, at a bad moment, with all the context to transfer; benefit: the response is run by whoever is best at running it, which need not be whoever noticed first. Or they may assign the Operations Lead role to someone else and stay in command — cost: they keep the coordination load and, unless they also delegate communications, the director too. The large worked case took the first option, transferring command before the scheduled shift handover specifically because the incoming person had more incident-response experience. (c) The working document, started once three or more people are working an incident. It lists working theories, eliminated causes, and useful debugging information such as error logs and suspect graphs, and its stated purpose is to preserve that information so it does not get lost in the conversation. With nineteen participants it is long overdue. (d) Move the detailed debugging into the shared document and keep the channel as the hub for decision making. That is exactly the split the large worked case adopted once discussion became too dense for the channel, and it works because the two kinds of traffic have different readers: detail is read by whoever picks up the thread, decisions must be read by everyone.

questions.prompt: A search service starts returning empty results for about a fifth of queries. Forty minutes in, the responders establish that every failing query is served from one of three sites in one continent, and that a configuration push went out to those sites shortly before the errors began — but they cannot yet say what in the configuration is wrong. The team lead's position is that pushing the previous configuration back would “undo a week of unrelated changes as well” and that they should keep reading the diff until they find the offending line. Two engineers are already writing a targeted patch, which they estimate at ninety minutes. (a) Give the four steps of an active incident in order, and say which step this team is on and which one they have skipped. (b) State the rule about details versus location, and apply it: is enough known to act, and on what evidence? (c) Take the team lead's objection at full strength, name what it correctly identifies, and say why it does not change the decision. (d) The targeted patch is not wasted work. Say what should happen to it and why, referring to what went wrong with the equivalent effort in the worked case.
questions.ideal: (a) The order is: 1. assess the impact; 2. mitigate the impact; 3. perform a root-cause analysis; 4. after the incident is over, fix what caused it and write a postmortem. Step 1 is done — a fifth of queries failing, localised to three sites. The team is working on step 3, and has skipped step 2 entirely. That inversion is the failure the whole ordering exists to prevent: first responders must prioritise mitigation above all else, or time to resolution suffers. (b) The rule is that to mitigate an incident you don't have to fully understand the details — you only need to know the location of the root cause. Enough is known. The failures are confined to three named sites in one continent, and a configuration push went to exactly those sites shortly before the errors began. That is a location plus a correlation with a recent change, which is precisely the situation the two canonical generic mitigations are for: roll back a recent release when an outage is correlated with the release cycle, or reconfigure load balancers to avoid a region when errors are localised. Both are available here. (c) The objection correctly identifies something real: generic mitigations are blunt instruments and may cause other disruptions to the service, and rolling back the configuration genuinely does undo a week of unrelated changes. It does not change the decision because that bluntness is the price of not needing a diagnosis, not an argument against paying it — the alternative on offer is another ninety minutes of a fifth of queries failing. Customers do not care whether you understand the outage; what they want is to stop receiving errors. The unrelated changes can be reapplied on a calm afternoon. (d) The targeted patch should continue in parallel, not instead. The error is running bespoke work as the only thing standing between users and the impact, and the worked case shows why: the equivalent effort there was a rebuild taking about an hour, which reached 90% completion before the team discovered another location using the bad path and had to restart the build. Bespoke work can be reset to zero by a single late discovery, and it cannot begin at all until the fault is understood. Note also that the rollback ends the impact but not the incident: mitigation is not prevention, so the investigation continues to root cause.

questions.prompt: A queue-backed notification system has now overflowed three times in a fortnight. Each time, an engineer has raised the consumer's memory limit, the backlog has drained, and the alert has cleared; nobody has found out why the backlog forms. A fourth occurrence lands on a Sunday, during a staged rollout that is at 60% and still progressing. The engineer who fixed it the previous three times is on holiday but answers a message and talks a colleague through it. (a) Name precisely what the three previous fixes achieved and what they did not. (b) Two decisions in this story are the same mistake as in the mishandled worked case. Name both, and give the specific corrective for each. (c) The holidaying engineer answered, so the incident was handled. Explain why this is recorded as a finding rather than a relief, and give the two structural alternatives. (d) Say what should be done with the rollout now, and what would have to be true before it resumes.
questions.ideal: (a) The three previous fixes mitigated the impact — the backlog drained and the alert cleared — and did nothing about recurrence, which requires the root cause. This is the mishandled worked case exactly: mitigation successfully stopped the impact on three separate occasions, each time by raising a quota, but the team could only prevent the issue from happening again once they discovered the root cause. Stopping the impact and stopping the repeat are different achievements, and only the second needs a diagnosis. (b) Two decisions repeat that case's mistakes. First, continuing the rollout after mitigating: after the first mitigation it would have been better to postpone the rollout until the root cause was fully determined, which is what avoids the eventual major disruption. The corrective is to hold the rollout until the cause is understood. Second, rolling out when the people who understand it are not available — the worked case's rollout reached 100% on a weekend, against the practice of performing rollouts only during business days so developers are around if something goes wrong. The corrective is to conduct rollouts during business hours. (c) Because successful incident management shouldn't rely on heroic efforts of individuals — the question that makes it a finding is what if they had been unreachable? The organisation was one unanswered message away from having no response at all, and the arrangement also taps someone during their own time, against a good work-life balance. The two structural alternatives are stated: conduct the rollouts during business hours, or organise an on-call rotation that provides paid coverage outside business hours. (d) Stop the rollout where it is. It should not resume until the root cause of the backlog is fully determined — and, given that this is the fourth occurrence, until whatever the root cause turns out to be has an owned fix rather than another limit increase. When it does resume, it should resume on a business day with the people who understand the system available.

questions.prompt: A sixty-person engineering organisation has a well-written incident response policy on its internal wiki, revised last year. During a genuine outage last month: the responders spent eleven minutes deciding between two chat tools and a video call; the on-call engineer wrote a customer-facing status update from scratch, which a manager then rewrote twice before it was published forty minutes later; nobody could find the escalation contact for the payments team; and two engineers argued for a quarter of an hour about whether the event qualified as an incident at all. The postmortem's single action item reads “re-read the incident policy”. (a) Name the four things that should have been settled in advance, matching each to the specific delay it would have removed here. (b) For the channel and the templates, give the stated reason each must be decided beforehand rather than chosen well in the moment. (c) Explain what is wrong with the action item, using the distinction between documentation and preparation. (d) The criteria argument is the most consequential of the four delays. Say why, and say where the criteria should come from.
questions.ideal: (a) Four things should have been settled in advance, and each maps to one delay. The communication channel — agreed and practised beforehand — removes the eleven minutes spent choosing between tools. Two or three ready-to-use templates, with the on-call knowing how to send them and the review and approval route agreed, remove the forty minutes of drafting and rewriting. A prepared list of contacts to email or page removes the search for the payments escalation. And established criteria for what counts as an incident remove the quarter-hour argument. (b) For the channel: no Incident Commander wants to make this decision during an incident — and the further instruction is to practise using it so there are no surprises, and to prefer one the team is already familiar with, because familiarity is what removes hesitation. For the templates: no one wants to write these announcements under extreme stress with no guidelines. Neither reason is about quality of judgement; both are about the cost of deciding at all at the worst moment. (c) “Re-read the incident policy” mistakes documentation for preparation. A document tells people what they should do; practice determines what they will do. Staying calm and following a response structure during an emergency takes practice, and practice builds muscle memory, which is what supplies confidence in a real emergency. Re-reading rehearses nothing and closes none of the four gaps. The correct action items are the four concrete decisions above, plus a drill and — crucially — the report that follows it. (d) The criteria argument is the most consequential because it delays the declaration itself, and everything else in the response exists only after that: the command line, the roles, the shared channel, the record. A team that cannot agree whether an event qualifies cannot declare early, so the whole structure arrives late. The criteria should be derived by looking at past outages and taking known high-risk areas into consideration — which this organisation, having had the outage described, is now in a position to do.

questions.prompt: A team wants to start practising incident response but has no budget for anything elaborate. They propose a quarterly exercise in which the on-call engineer is given a written scenario and talks through what they would do, in a meeting, for twenty minutes. There is no report afterwards — the group discusses it and moves on. Separately, during a real nine-hour incident last week, the same commander ran the whole response because “she had all the context”, and by hour seven the team was re-testing hypotheses it had already eliminated. (a) Give the three scales of drill available, and say which of them this team could run this week at no cost. (b) Name what their proposed exercise is missing that would make it preparation rather than conversation, and say what specifically that missing piece produces. (c) Their scenario is invented from scratch each time. Give the better source and say why. (d) Address the nine-hour incident: name the practice that was skipped, give both of its stated benefits, and say which one would have prevented the repeated hypotheses.
questions.ideal: (a) Three scales are available: a company-wide resilience test, which creates a controlled emergency that does not actually impact customers and which teams respond to as if it were real; a role-playing exercise in which engineers reenact a previous incident in its documented roles; and intentionally treating minor problems as major ones requiring a large-scale response, which lets the team practise with the real procedures and tools in a real-world situation at lower stakes. The third costs nothing and can be run this week, on the next minor problem that arrives; the role-play is nearly as cheap if any postmortems exist. (b) What is missing is the report afterwards, detailing what went well, what didn't, and how things could have been handled better. Its product is the list of gaps in incident management: the most valuable part of running a drill is examining the outcomes, because once you know what the gaps are you can work toward closing them. Without it the exercise is a conversation that leaves no trace, which is also why drills are far more useful when run periodically rather than once. (c) Build the scenario from a postmortem — postmortems contain plenty of ideas for incident management drills. They describe failures the system has actually produced rather than ones somebody imagined, they come with a known account of what happened for comparison, and they reuse work already done. Two related instructions: use real tools as much as possible, and consider breaking your test environment so the team performs real troubleshooting. (d) The skipped practice is rotating responders, including the commander — one organisation rotated both every four hours through an incident that ran past ten hours. Its two stated benefits are different in kind: it encouraged engineers to get rest, and it brought new ideas into the response team. The second is what would have prevented hour seven's re-testing of an eliminated hypothesis, since the person who eliminated it seven hours ago is the least likely person to notice they are doing it again. (The shared working document guards the same failure from the other direction, by recording what has already been ruled out.)

questions.prompt: Here is the whole Lessons Learned section of a postmortem for a six-hour billing outage. “Things that went poorly: nobody on the platform team had documented the failover procedure, which is frankly astonishing for a service this old. Priya was on call and did not escalate for two hours. Where we got lucky: the batch job hadn't started yet — I don't want to think about what would have happened otherwise!” The action items are: “Make failover more reliable” (P2, no owner, no ticket); “Improve on-call training so people escalate sooner” (P2, no owner, no ticket); “Document the failover runbook” (P2, owner: Priya, ticket BUG-4471). The document lists five owners and was shared with the platform team. (a) Identify every distinct failure mode present, naming each. (b) For the blame, state the mechanism by which it damages the organisation — and say why that mechanism makes this a practical problem rather than an etiquette one. (c) Rewrite the three action items so they satisfy every stated characteristic of a good one, and say which one you would delete outright and why. (d) Two structural facts are given at the end. Name what is wrong with each and what it should be instead.
questions.ideal: (a) Seven distinct failure modes. Counterproductive finger pointing: a named individual identified as not having escalated, and the platform team blamed for the missing documentation. Animated language: “frankly astonishing” and the exclamation in “Where we got lucky” — a postmortem is a factual artifact that should be free from personal judgements and subjective language. Weak action items, with four separate defects: ambiguous phrasing (“Make failover more reliable”, “Improve on-call training”) that is open to interpretation and unmeasurable; all items at equal priority, so there is no way to determine which to tackle first; missing owners on two of three; and only one tracking bug. An action item aimed at humans rather than systems. Missing ownership: five owners on the document. Limited audience: shared with the platform team alone. There is also no impact data anywhere in the section shown, which is key details omitted. (b) Highlighting individuals leads team members to become risk-averse because they're afraid of being publicly shamed, and — the part that matters operationally — they may be motivated to cover up facts critical to understanding and preventing recurrence. That makes it a practical problem rather than an etiquette one: the cost is not hurt feelings but missing information in the next postmortem, which is the document you will need to prevent the next outage. Naming Priya here buys nothing and quietly degrades every future write-up in the organisation. (c) Rewritten, each with a single owner, a priority, a tracking bug and a verifiable end state, and aimed at the system: “Add an automated failover exercise to the weekly release pipeline that fails the build if failover exceeds N minutes” — P1, one owner, ticket. “Page the secondary on-call automatically when an incident is unmitigated after 30 minutes” — P1, one owner, ticket. “Write the failover runbook and validate it by executing it end to end in a drill” — P1, one owner, ticket. The item to delete outright is “improve on-call training so people escalate sooner”: trying to change human behavior is less reliable than changing automated systems and processes, so it is replaced by the automatic escalation above rather than kept. Note also that this was a user-affecting outage, so at least one item should be P0 or P1. And the runbook item's owner should be whoever will do the work, not the person who was on call. (d) The five owners should be one owner and multiple collaborators — a single point of contact responsible for the postmortem, the follow-up and the completion, because declaring official ownership results in accountability, which leads to action. The platform-team-only audience should be everyone at the company by default, shared as widely as possible and perhaps even with customers, because the value of a postmortem is proportional to the learning it creates.

questions.prompt: A director notices three things over six months. Postmortems for that org are consistently published seven to ten weeks after the incident. In a review meeting a vice-president said, “Look, blameless is fine in principle, but someone in that room clearly knew this was risky — why did nobody speak up?” And a team has now had three outages with near-identical causes, each with a completed postmortem and every action item closed. (a) For the publication delay, give both harms, and name the underlying organisational cause along with the rule about quality bars. (b) Give a specific reply to the vice-president that redirects the conversation without contradicting them, and state the principle about good faith and information that justifies it. (c) The third observation is the strangest: closed action items and recurring outages. Give the questions to ask, and say what it means when the items are all closing on time. (d) Name two incentives the director could introduce that target closeout and organisational learning rather than authorship, and say what each is designed to prevent.
questions.ideal: (a) Two harms. A prompt postmortem tends to be more accurate because information is fresh in the contributors' minds, so a seven-to-ten-week delay loses detail — and had the worked case's outage recurred while its weak document was still pending, which the outage did in reality do, the team would likely have forgotten details a timely one would have captured. And the people affected are waiting for an explanation and a demonstration that you have things under control: the longer you wait, the more they will fill the gap with the products of their imagination, which seldom works in your favour. The underlying cause named is lacking time to write postmortems: quality postmortems take time, and when a team is overloaded the quality suffers, producing subpar documents with incomplete action items that make recurrence far more likely. On quality bars: postmortems are letters you write to future team members, so it is very important to keep a consistent bar, lest you accidentally teach future teammates a bad lesson. The remedy is to prioritise postmortem work, track completion and review, and allow teams adequate time to implement the action plan. (b) Something close to: “I'm sure everyone had the best intent, so to keep it blameless, maybe we ask generically whether there were any warning signs we could have heeded, and why we might have dismissed them.” It moves the narrative in a more constructive direction without contradicting the vice-president. The justifying principle is that individuals act in good faith and make decisions based on the best information available, so investigating the source of misleading information is much more beneficial to the organisation than assigning blame — the interesting question is why the warning did not reach the people deciding, which is a system question. (c) Repeating incidents mean it is time to dig deeper, and the questions are: are action items taking too long to close? Is feature velocity trumping reliability fixes? Are the right action items being captured in the first place? Is the faulty service overdue for a refactor? Are people putting sticking plasters on a more serious problem? When every item is closing on time, the first question is answered and the remaining ones become the live ones — most pointedly whether the right items were ever captured, and whether the service needs a refactor rather than more patches. Having uncovered a systemic process or technical problem, step back and consider overall service health, and bring the postmortem collaborators from each similar incident together to decide the course of action. (d) Two that target closeout and learning rather than authorship. Reward action item closeout explicitly, keeping incentives balanced between writing the postmortem and successfully implementing its action plan — this prevents the unvirtuous cycle of unclosed postmortems you get from rewarding the writing alone. And gamification: a scoreboard or burndown of open action items, of the kind used in twice-yearly fix-it weeks where those who close the most receive recognition — this prevents items ageing invisibly by making the backlog itself public. Equally acceptable: rewarding the resulting organisational change with peer bonuses, positive reviews or promotion, which prevents learning staying inside one team; and holding postmortem owners up as experts, which counteracts people avoiding association with a write-up.

questions.prompt: Define resolving an incident and managing an incident, give the four basic principles of incident response, and say what a pre-agreed structure is actually protecting.
questions.ideal: Resolving an incident means mitigating its impact and/or restoring the service to the condition it was in before. Managing one means coordinating the efforts of the responding teams efficiently, and making sure communication flows in both directions — between the responders themselves, and outward to everyone with an interest in how the incident is progressing. The four basic principles: keep one clear line of command; give the roles clear definitions; maintain a working record of the debugging and the mitigation while you do it; and declare incidents both early and often. What a pre-agreed structure protects is attention. Large-scale incidents are confusing, and a structure the team has settled on beforehand reduces that chaos; formulating the rules for communicating and coordinating before disaster strikes is what lets the team concentrate on resolving the problem when one occurs. A team that has already practised and familiarised itself with those rules does not have to spend any of its thinking on them during the emergency.

questions.prompt: Give the three Cs, say what they are goals for and what they are not, and state where the culprit usually lies when a response goes wrong.
questions.ideal: Coordinate the response effort; communicate between the incident responders, within the organisation, and to the outside world; and maintain control over the incident response. They are the goals every incident response framework has in common, and they are goals for the response rather than for the system — none of them is about repairing the fault, which is why a response can resolve a problem quickly and still have failed at all three. Mastering them is described as essential to responding effectively. And when something goes wrong with incident response, the culprit is likely to be found in one of those three areas, which makes them a diagnostic list as well as a set of aims.

questions.prompt: Name the three main roles, say how they are organised, give the default rule about roles that have not been delegated, and say which role can be absorbed back and under what condition.
questions.ideal: The Incident Commander, the Operations Lead and the Communications Lead. They are organised as a hierarchy: the commander leads the response, and the other two report to them. The commander directs the high-level state of the incident, commands and coordinates it, delegates roles as needed, communicates, stays in control and works with the other responders toward resolution; the operations lead applies operational tools to mitigate or resolve the problem; the communications lead is the public face, giving periodic updates to the response team and to stakeholders and handling inquiries about the incident. The default rule is that the commander assumes every role that has not yet been delegated, so no part of the work is ever unowned — and the person who declares the incident typically steps into the commander role. The elastic role is communications: if the incident becomes small enough, that role can be subsumed back into the commander's. Both leads may run teams of their own, and those teams expand or contract as the incident requires.

questions.prompt: Give the three specific benefits of declaring an incident early, and explain why declaring should be understood as creating the response rather than escalating it.
questions.ideal: Declaring early ensures three things. Miscommunication between the separate groups working the problem is prevented. Root-cause identification and resolution happen sooner. And relevant teams are looped in earlier, which makes communication to the outside world faster and smoother. It is described as creating the response rather than escalating it because everything a managed incident consists of comes into being at that moment: the line of command, the defined roles, the single place where everyone talks, and the record kept as the work proceeds. Until the declaration, there is a group of individuals and a ticket. That is why the principle is to declare early and often, and why the observation that managed incidents are resolved faster is an argument for lowering the threshold rather than for being sure first — the three benefits above are forfeited by waiting, not merely postponed.

questions.prompt: Give the four steps of an active incident in order, say which is top priority and what happens if it is not, and state the rule about details versus location.
questions.ideal: The order is: assess the impact of the incident; mitigate the impact; perform a root-cause analysis; and, once the incident is over, fix whatever caused it and write a postmortem. Afterwards you can run drills against the vulnerabilities the incident exposed, and engineers can work on projects to address them. Mitigation is the top priority, and the consequence of treating it otherwise is stated plainly — a first responder who puts anything above mitigating will see the time to resolution suffer for it. The enabling rule: mitigating an incident does not require you to understand the details in full, only to know whereabouts the root cause lies. That is what makes acting before diagnosis possible, and the capacity to mitigate while the cause remains unexplained is called crucial for running robust services at high availability. Customers do not care whether you understand what caused the outage; what they want is to stop receiving errors.

questions.prompt: Define a generic mitigation, give two examples, state the price it carries, and say when the tooling for one should be built and how you find out which tooling you need.
questions.ideal: A generic mitigation is something a first responder does to relieve the pain while the root cause is still not fully understood. Two examples: rolling back a recent release when an outage correlates with the release cycle, and reconfiguring load balancers to steer away from a region when the errors are localised there. The price is that they are blunt instruments and may disrupt other parts of the service — their impact is broader than a precise solution's — but they go in fast and stop the bleeding while the team is still working out what the underlying cause is and dealing with it. The tooling that makes such an action quick does take engineering time to develop, and general-purpose mitigation tools should be built ahead of any incident rather than in the middle of responding to one. To find out which tools you actually need, browse your existing postmortems: they are a good way to discover the mitigations and tools that would have been useful in retrospect, so you can build them into services and manage the next incident better.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between mitigating an incident and preventing its recurrence, using the case where the impact was stopped three times, and say what should have happened to the rollout.
questions.ideal: Mitigating stops the impact; preventing recurrence requires the root cause, and only the second is achieved by understanding what happened. In the case where a quota was raised, mitigation successfully stopped the impact on three separate occasions, and on each occasion the problem returned — the team could only stop it recurring once they had found the underlying defect. The general policy is to stop the impact of an incident first and find the root cause afterwards, unless the cause happens to be identified early on; but once the impact is mitigated, understanding the cause is just as important, precisely so the issue does not happen again. What should have happened to the rollout is that it should have been postponed after the first mitigation, until the root cause had been fully determined. Continuing it instead is what led to the major disruption later, when the release reached every device over a weekend and users lost half of their requests.

questions.prompt: Name the four things to settle before an incident, give the stated reason for two of them, and give the two symmetrical assumptions people make when you tell them nothing.
questions.ideal: Settle the communication channel, two or three ready-to-use announcement templates, a prepared list of people to email or page, and an established set of criteria for deciding whether a paging issue is really an incident. The channel must be agreed and practised in advance because no Incident Commander wants to be making that decision during an incident — and it is better to pick one the team is already familiar with, so everyone is comfortable using it. The templates must exist in advance because nobody wants to be writing public announcements under extreme stress with no guidelines; the drafting, review, approval and release path should be thought through at the same time. The two assumptions people make in the absence of information are symmetrical. If you do not acknowledge that an incident is happening and is actively being addressed, they will automatically assume that nothing is being done about it. And if you forget to call off the response once the problem has been mitigated or resolved, they will assume the incident is still going on. Both are preempted by regular status updates, and the second means that closing an incident is an announcement rather than merely a state.

questions.prompt: Give the three scales of incident drill, say what makes a drill worth running and what makes one worthless, and give the two reasons for rotating responders during a long incident.
questions.ideal: Three scales. A company-wide resilience test, in which a controlled emergency that does not actually affect customers is created and teams respond to it as though it were real, reviewing the response procedures afterwards. A smaller role-playing exercise, in which engineers rehearse a specific past incident. And the cheapest of the three: deliberately handling a minor problem as though it were a major one demanding a full-scale response, so the team exercises the actual procedures and tools in a genuine situation where the stakes are low. What makes a drill worth running is that it is run periodically and followed by a report detailing what went well, what did not, and how things could have been handled better — examining the outcomes is the most valuable part, because it reveals the gaps in incident management, and once you know what those are you can work toward closing them. A drill with no such review is exercise rather than preparation. Build scenarios from postmortems, which contain plenty of ideas, use real tools as far as possible, and consider breaking a test environment so the troubleshooting is genuine. The two reasons for rotating responders and the commander during a long incident — one organisation rotated both every four hours through a ten-hour response — are that it encourages engineers to get rest, and that it brings new ideas into the response team.

questions.prompt: Give the four characteristics of a good action item, state the rule about changing humans versus changing systems, and explain the mechanism by which blame in a postmortem damages the next one.
questions.ideal: The four are ownership, prioritisation, measurability and preventative action. Ownership covers two things at once — every item carries both an owner and a tracking number. Prioritisation means every item is given a priority level rather than all sharing one. Measurability means the item has a verifiable end state, so 'add an alert when more than a given percentage of our machines have been taken away from us' qualifies and 'improve the alerting' does not. And preventative action means each theme of items contains work that helps avoid the outage recurring, not only work that makes it survivable. Without a formal tracking process, action items are often simply forgotten, which results in further outages. The rule about people is that trying to change human behaviour is less reliable than changing automated systems and processes, so an item proposing to make humans less error-prone should be replaced by one that changes what the system will accept. Blame damages the next postmortem through a specific mechanism. Singling people out makes the rest of the team risk-averse, because nobody wants to be shamed in public next, and it gives them a motive to conceal exactly the facts that are critical to understanding the incident and stopping it recurring. So the cost is not hurt feelings but missing information in the very document you will need next time — which is why blamelessness is a practical requirement rather than a courtesy, and why it coexists with naming a single owner for the document and for every action item.

retired.reason: Part (a) read 'using the distinction the source draws', which points at a text outside the booklet and breaks the no-meta rule. Reissued with the pointer removed.
retired.prompt_fragment: Name precisely what the three previous fixes achieved and what they did not, using the distinction the source draws.
retired.ideal: (a) The three previous fixes mitigated the impact — the backlog drained and the alert cleared — and did nothing about recurrence, which requires the root cause. This is the mishandled worked case exactly: mitigation successfully stopped the impact on three separate occasions, each time by raising a quota, but the team could only prevent the issue from happening again once they discovered the root cause. Stopping the impact and stopping the repeat are different achievements, and only the second needs a diagnosis. (b) Two decisions repeat that case's mistakes. First, continuing the rollout after mitigating: after the first mitigation it would have been better to postpone the rollout until the root cause was fully determined, which is what avoids the eventual major disruption. The corrective is to hold the rollout until the cause is understood. Second, rolling out when the people who understand it are not available — the worked case's rollout reached 100% on a weekend, against the practice of performing rollouts only during business days so developers are around if something goes wrong. The corrective is to conduct rollouts during business hours. (c) Because successful incident management shouldn't rely on heroic efforts of individuals — the question that makes it a finding is what if they had been unreachable? The organisation was one unanswered message away from having no response at all, and the arrangement also taps someone during their own time, against a good work-life balance. The two structural alternatives are stated: conduct the rollouts during business hours, or organise an on-call rotation that provides paid coverage outside business hours. (d) Stop the rollout where it is. It should not resume until the root cause of the backlog is fully determined — and, given that this is the fourth occurrence, until whatever the root cause turns out to be has an owned fix rather than another limit increase. When it does resume, it should resume on a business day with the people who understand the system available.

And the people affected are waiting for an explanation and a demonstration that you have things under control: the longer you wait, the more they will fill the gap with the products of their imagination, which seldom works in your favour. The underlying cause named is lacking time to write postmortems: quality postmortems take time, and when a team is overloaded the quality suffers, producing subpar documents with incomplete action items that make recurrence far more likely. The remedy is to prioritise postmortem work, track completion and review, and allow teams adequate time to implement the action plan. When every item is closing on time, the first question is answered and the remaining ones become the live ones — most pointedly whether the right items were ever captured, and whether the service needs a refactor rather than more patches. competencies.title: Large-Scale Change & Deprecation — Constraint, Economics, Machinery, Removal
parts: Why one big commit stops working

questions.prompt: A platform team needs to rename a configuration key used in roughly 40,000 files across one repository. Their first attempt — a single commit — was rejected by the version control server after twenty minutes. Their second attempt succeeded locally but failed to land because eleven files had changed underneath them. A colleague suggests scheduling the third attempt for 3 a.m. on a public holiday. Separately, about 300 of the affected files belong to a billing service written six years ago whose last maintainer left the company; the team's own instinct is to skip those files and file a ticket. (a) Define a large-scale change, and say whether this qualifies and on what grounds. (b) Name the barrier behind each of the two failed attempts, and give the stated remedy for each. (c) Assess the 3 a.m. proposal: say what it is a version of, and the precise condition under which it stops working. (d) Name what the billing service is, say why skipping it is worse than it looks, and give the one thing that dissolves it.
questions.ideal: (a) A large-scale change is any set of changes that are logically related but cannot practically be submitted as a single atomic unit. This qualifies on both of the stated grounds at once: it touches so many files that the underlying tooling cannot commit them all, and it is large enough that it would always have merge conflicts. Note that it qualifies because of the impossibility of atomicity, not because 40,000 is a big number. (b) The first failure is a technical limitation: most version control systems have operations that scale linearly with the size of a change, and a system that handles tens of files may lack the memory or processing power to atomically commit thousands — in centralised systems such commits can also block other writers while they process. The remedy is to split the change into smaller independent chunks, accepting that this makes execution more complex. The second is merge conflicts: every version control system requires updating and merging if a newer version of a file exists centrally, and the probability of hitting that grows with the number of files in the change, compounded by the number of engineers working in the repository. The remedy is the same shape — with few files in a change, the probability shrinks. (c) The 3 a.m. proposal is the small-company manoeuvre: sneaking in a change that touches every file at a time when nobody is developing, or holding an informal global lock by passing a virtual — or even physical — token around the team. It stops working at exactly the point where somebody is always making changes to the repository, which is the normal condition of a large or globally distributed organisation. (d) The billing service is a haunted graveyard: a system so ancient, obtuse or complex that no one dares enter it, typically business-critical, frozen in time because any change might make it fail in incomprehensible ways, and often wrapped in layers of bureaucracy to prevent destabilising changes. Skipping it is worse than it looks because these are anathema to the whole process: they prevent the completion of large migrations, the decommissioning of other systems that rely on them, and the upgrade of compilers or libraries they use — from this perspective they prevent all kinds of meaningful progress, and the harm is to other people's work rather than to the team that owns them. The one thing that dissolves it is thorough testing: when software is thoroughly tested, arbitrary changes can be made to it and you will know with confidence whether they break it, no matter the age or complexity of the system.

questions.prompt: Two migrations are proposed in the same quarter. The first replaces a logging call across 9,000 files; the team plans one change and reports that a test three layers away in the dependency graph failed, which they have spent two days investigating. The second is the same edit across 60 files in a subsystem where every project uses a different formatter, a different CI configuration and two different version control systems. A director asks why the second one — a fiftieth of the size — is being quoted as the harder job, and proposes that both be split into 200-file commits to “standardise the approach”. (a) Explain the first team's two days using what is said about the dependency graph, and say what change to their approach would have prevented it. (b) Answer the director's question: name the barrier the second migration is hitting and why size does not govern it. (c) Evaluate the 200-file proposal for each migration separately. (d) Splitting has a stated cost and produces a stated inefficiency. Name both, and give the reasoning by which the inefficiency is accepted.
questions.ideal: (a) The continuous-integration system runs not only the tests immediately impacted by a change but every test that transitively depends on the changed files, which gives broad coverage — and the farther away in the dependency graph a test is from the impacted files, the more unlikely a failure is to have been caused by the change itself. Two days on a three-layers-away failure is therefore the expected outcome rather than bad luck. What would have prevented it is smaller independent changes: each affects a smaller set of tests, and failures are easier to diagnose and fix. Finding the root cause of a failure in a change of 25 files is straightforward; finding one in a 10,000-file change is the proverbial needle in a haystack. (b) The second migration is hitting heterogeneity. These changes work only when the bulk of the effort can be done by computers rather than humans, and computers rely on consistent environments to apply the proper transformations to the correct places; many different version control systems, continuous-integration systems, project-specific tooling or formatting guidelines make sweeping changes difficult. Size does not govern it because the obstacle scales with the number of distinct environments, not the number of files — 60 files spread across several incompatible setups needs several solutions, while 9,000 files in one consistent setup needs one. (c) For the first migration, splitting into 200-file commits is exactly right: it addresses the version-control limits, reduces the conflict probability, and makes failures diagnosable. For the second it accomplishes nothing, because the barrier is not change size; the remedy there is to simplify the environment — embracing some of the complexity by making it standard across the codebase, and asking teams to omit their special checks where the shards touch their project code. Most teams are happy to help, given the benefit. (d) The cost of splitting is that it makes the execution of the change more complex. The inefficiency it produces is that smaller changes cause the same tests to be run multiple times, particularly tests that depend on large parts of the codebase. It is accepted because engineer time spent tracking down test failures is much more expensive than the compute time required to run those extra tests — a conscious decision, and one explicitly flagged as a trade-off that might not hold for every organisation.
