The concrete method: when you think of a solution, treat it as “just the first” and spend at least the same amount of time on another, and now that you understand the problem better see if you can make it simpler — fewer lines of code, fewer branches, fewer teams, fewer hours of maintenance, fewer running components, fewer files touched; the longer the system is intended to last, the longer you should spend. Where complexity is genuinely inherent, make a deliberate decision about where in the system to put it, so that someone looking at the whole can treat that component as a black box and reason about everything else. (b) The hard-coded calls will cost whoever has to replace or remove the service, and the practice that answers it is building to decommission. Your architecture will evolve and your components will settle into the middle; while it might be faster now to wire the new thing straight in, ask whether it will be possible to replace it later without demolishing whatever other people have built on top of it. The test: imagine knowing that you personally will need to decommission this component in ten years, and that Future You will be no less busy than Present You — so add a clean interface, make it easy to see which clients are still using it, and design in a way that keeps a little distance between two systems being integrated. The side effect is the payoff: if you set out from the start to build a component that is easy to decommission, you will have built something modular and easy to maintain. (c) There are two options for letting future people understand a system. One is to focus on education and hands-on experience — running continual classes so that everyone who might have to work on it is fully trained and has logged enough hours to handle problems. The other is to make it as easy as possible for people to understand it when they need to: documentation written with that future person as the main audience — a clear, short introduction; at least one big, simple picture, using arrows to show which direction data moves; links to anything they might wonder about — and then exposing the system's inner workings as clearly as possible through tooling, tracing or useful status messages, so that it is easy to inspect, analyse and debug. By offering to explain it to anyone who asks, this team has implicitly chosen the first, and the reason that fails is that the system will never again be as well understood as it is on the day it is created, with that knowledge decaying a little every day. On the backups the position is unambiguous: if you have not tested restoring your backups, assume you do not have any. (d) The justification. Technical impressiveness is not a reason. You are working for an organisation that has goals, and the software is the means to those ends, not an end in itself; keep the idea of a budget in the back of your mind, and know how the company makes money and whether these are good times or lean ones. More sharply, headcount is finite and staffing a project has an opportunity cost, and you should be judicious about where you spend your innovation tokens — the organisation's limited capacity to do something creative, or weird, or hard. Build the most useful thing, not the thing that would be most fun to build, and when it is time to stop polishing something and declare it good enough, stop. In a freeze the justification has to be expressed in what the business needs. The behaviour during the incident. The relevant attribute is creating calm: if you are dealing with a big problem try to make it smaller, and if it is a small one keep it small. A senior person making a fuss can blow up a minor thing into a big, loud issue, so be certain you have the facts and that joining in genuinely helps — if your actions would amplify rather than calm, consider staying out of it. And be cautious about where you share your anxieties: do not let your worries spill out on more junior people — it is not fair to ask them to carry your concerns, and you are amplifying the problem if you upset them. Take the uncertainty instead to a manager, a close peer or a chosen sounding board, being clear whether you are asking for action or unpacking something for yourself, since otherwise the person may reflexively react and amplify what you meant only as venting.

questions.prompt: Name the four risks that come with depth in a domain, say which two are mirror images and what single cause produces both, and give the test for whether your current work is worth your time.
questions.ideal: Sustained focus on one area buys expertise and charges four specific taxes. You rank things wrongly, because when the people near you all care about the same set of concerns those concerns swell, outside problems shrink, and the peak visible from inside starts to feel like the summit — which is also why prior art goes unchecked, although a genuinely novel problem is rare. You stop extending sympathy to other disciplines, treating their work as something you could knock out over a weekend, which also colours your vocabulary, what you bother to spell out, and the motives you attribute to colleagues. You become blind to nearby faults, so the ugly configuration or the deploy process everyone works around no longer registers as anything to repair, and a situation drifting toward crisis is no longer something you can size accurately. And the link between the labour and its reason snaps: the effort carries on after its original purpose has died or been satisfied by some other route, everybody handles a fragment, no individual feels answerable for the outcome, and at the extreme the ethical dimension disappears from view. The first and third are opposite manifestations of one underlying cause — the sheer quantity of time spent immersed in a single domain — one inflating what is close and the other erasing it. The yardstick offered is not modesty: not working on the highest-priority item is acceptable, yet the work must not squander your time, and an inability to articulate to yourself why this task requires somebody of your seniority is a signal that you have picked up the wrong task.

questions.prompt: Explain why paying attention is not sufficient for knowing what is going on, name the second requirement, and give three of the six standing ways to keep an organisational picture current.
questions.ideal: Noticing is only one of two ingredients. The trainable half is habitual alertness — filtering signal from the surrounding chatter and teaching yourself to register a fact as interesting and retain it, writing facts down if your memory does not hold them naturally. The half that noticing cannot supply is reach: you have to be present for, or downstream of, the conversations and rulings that bear on your work, and there is a great deal you will never think to request because you have no idea it exists. Two people with identical powers of observation can therefore hold completely different pictures of the same organisation, and the fix for one deficiency does nothing for the other. Six habits keep the picture from going stale, any three of which count: subscribing to feeds and channels that broadcast new designs, outages and change tickets; going out to where the work happens, by pairing on a change, handling an incident, or running a deployment, which also protects your technical credibility rather than merely your context; reading material that is not addressed to you, such as senior colleagues' calendars, the notes of meetings you skip, and the roster of channels ordered by creation date so that new efforts announce themselves; setting aside calendar time to skim or study written proposals; maintaining sponsors and allies who will pass on what is happening behind the curtain; and simply having conversations, particularly outside engineering, where support staff and administrators know more about what you built and who is doing what than anyone in your own function.

questions.prompt: List the seven attributes on which organisational personality is described, and give one example of a single behaviour that is virtuous at one end of an attribute and disqualifying at the other.
questions.ideal: The seven axes are how much is disclosed versus hoarded; whether decisions travel by speech or by document; whether direction descends from leadership or wells up from teams; whether the place pivots quickly or moves with deliberation; whether work is unlocked through informal contacts or through published request routes; whether people's time is fully committed or largely uncommitted; and whether status and position are fluid or locked into a stable lattice. Most organisations land near the centre of each, and either extreme makes manoeuvring hard. A worked example of one act reversing verdict: passing on something a manager told you privately destroys their confidence in you where information is treated as currency, whereas sitting on the same information marks you as scheming or unreliable where everything is expected to be visible. A second example works equally well — recording a decision in a document earns you a reputation for sloppiness if you omit it in a deliberate, paper-driven environment, and earns you pushback for slowing everyone down in a place that settles matters in corridors, where anything past a page goes unread. What the organisation prints as its values is aspiration; the operative values are visible in daily conduct.

questions.prompt: Name the five terrain features that obstruct or assist a route, give the distinct remedy each takes, and say what most gatekeepers are actually motivated by.
questions.ideal: Five landmarks, and no two are cleared the same way. Gaps between organisations, and the ragged seams where two teams' stated duties fail to meet, swallow work and information; you close them by carrying the message across yourself — writing the recap nobody writes, connecting two people who should already have met, producing the document that shows how the pieces relate. A person or group who will not let anything through is passed by arriving with backing from somebody they hold in regard, or by satisfying whatever conditions they demand: evidence every risk is handled, completed forms and capacity figures, satisfactory replies to every comment. Ground claimed by several teams at once, where each will vouch only for its own slice and refers you onward, requires that a single party be made answerable for the entire thing before you proceed, or you will have to acquire that whole picture yourself. A contest everybody has written off as hopeless is not forbidden, but attempting it demands proof that your attempt differs from the failures before it. And official routes that have been engineered to be the path of least resistance should be used when they exist — while remembering that the sanctioned procedure is sometimes precisely the one experienced people have learned to bypass, so establish which route actually carries the traffic. On motive: the overwhelming majority of those who block progress are not petty tyrants but people acting out of concern, guarding architectural or code quality and trying to keep everybody out of trouble.

questions.prompt: Give the five consequences of a group having no long-term destination, and set out both branches of the mechanism by which such a group ends up with unmaintainable systems.
questions.ideal: Without an agreed endpoint, five things follow. Holding a common heading becomes laborious, since teams either aim somewhere unhelpful or turn every choice into a protracted debate. Ambitious work never lands, because anything demanding several successive stages loses to immediate local irritations, and outsiders cannot see what the current efforts are worth. Systems fill with residue. Rival campaigns spring up, with different people each recruiting support for a different heading, all acting in good faith and collectively producing disorder. And the engineers themselves stall, because a group fed short, tightly specified assignments never develops the capacity to spot and close the gaps between tasks, nor the ability to narrate why it did what it did. The residue arrives by exactly two routes, which is why opposite conduct yields the same wreckage. A team may attempt to accommodate every conceivable future, and what it produces is elaborate and painful to keep alive. Or it may settle the question locally on its own authority, gambling that its choice aligns with everyone else's, and when it does not the result is an oddity that every other team must permanently work around.

questions.prompt: List the eight things you must find out before a large project can be said to have started, say which of them can legitimately end the project, and explain why counting produced code is a defective measure of progress.
questions.ideal: Eight things have to be pinned down: the reason the work is happening at all; what the people who will use the output actually need; the yardstick by which the result will be judged; who is funding it, who has a stake and who the customers are; the limits that genuinely cannot move; what could derail it; what came before, including abandoned attempts and the feelings left behind; and who is involved, including the other leaders and what role each expects to occupy. The first of these can terminate the effort: once you grasp why it is being done, you may conclude that the thing you have been handed will not deliver the outcome it is meant to, and finishing it would consume everybody's time for nothing — better discovered at the outset. Counting produced code fails as a gauge because written code is not evidence that any problem has been resolved; occasionally the outcome that constitutes success is removing code rather than adding it, and in any case the figure reports the team's own activity instead of the difference made to anyone. There is a matching warning for anyone measuring their own initiative: reputation and goodwill can carry a project for a while on the strength of belief in you, but you cannot be sure you are correct, so apply the harshest scepticism to your own proposals and establish observable targets early.

questions.prompt: Give the four responsibilities in the assignment matrix with the numerical constraint attached to one of them, name the two dysfunctions it is meant to remove, and say what its real advantage is.
questions.ideal: The four labels are the person performing the work; the person who ultimately hands it over and puts their name to its completion, of whom exactly one is permitted per item and who is frequently the same individual performing it; those whose views are solicited; and those merely kept abreast of progress. It removes two recognisable dysfunctions: a group that talks indefinitely because nobody can identify who is entitled to settle the matter, and a group that keeps reopening settled questions for want of any agreed procedure for settling them. Its genuine merit is not the grid but its blandness — it is a sufficiently neutral, uncontentious device that you can raise the question of who decides without the conversation becoming personal or awkward. Lay it out when the work begins rather than after two people find themselves duplicating each other or after something falls through because no one believed it was theirs. And note the residual clause: whoever leads is quietly occupying every post that has been left vacant — growth of the people, capture of requirements, the project-management function — which accumulates into a substantial load.

questions.prompt: State how you can tell that a team has not investigated its problem enough, list the headings no design document may omit, and give both techniques for making prose unambiguous.
questions.ideal: The diagnostic is the shape of the stated aim: when a group cannot express what it is after, or when its stated aim turns out to be a restatement of the thing it plans to build, the investigation stage has been cut short. A properly investigated problem yields a short pitch, an account of each participating team's wants that they will endorse as accurate, and an explicit boundary listing what is excluded. Regardless of how slight the document, five headings are mandatory: the framing details that place it in time and identify it, including a status; the purpose; the proposed approach in sufficient detail to be judged workable; the handling of protection, privacy and regulatory obligations, which must state the reasoning even when you believe none apply; and the options you weighed or the work already done elsewhere, whose absence — particularly if the absence is because you weighed none — betrays insufficient thought. Two devices remove ambiguity from the prose. Attach a doer to every action, since constructions with no subject leave the reader guessing at who performs it, and rewrite them so a named party does the thing. And spend the extra words: rather than a naked demonstrative pronoun, restate the noun it stands for even when you mentioned it a moment earlier, because repetition is cheaper than the ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Name the four qualities a senior engineer models involuntarily, say what most reliably reveals what an organisation truly rewards, and explain why declaring ignorance is more valuable coming from an experienced person.
questions.ideal: The four are capability, adult responsibility, holding on to the purpose, and thinking beyond the present moment. They are set out as things to aim at rather than a threshold that certifies you, and the material explicitly says that where its counsel conflicts with your own judgement you should back yourself, since recognising when received wisdom is mistaken is part of the role. What discloses an organisation's genuine priorities is who it elevates: a stated commitment to working together collapses if solitary heroics are the route to advancement, and a written expectation of careful examination of changes evaporates the moment experienced people wave changes through unread, because the rest of the group will follow suit. Confessing ignorance carries more weight from a veteran for two connected reasons. It costs the veteran least — the field is thick with ego and insecurity, and for a newer engineer conceding a gap can be frightening or genuinely hazardous, so the person who can afford the admission should make it. And the admission travels: once experienced people demonstrate that not knowing is ordinary, the rest do it too, which matters because so much of working life is spent assembling a common picture of reality in order to decide and cooperate, and that assembly stalls whenever participants pretend or quietly withdraw rather than risk exposure.

questions.prompt: Explain the two advantages of announcing an action in advance over requesting approval for it, describe why unassigned coordination work damages the career of whoever absorbs it, and give the exercise that produces a component someone can later switch off.
questions.ideal: Flagging a move ahead of making it does two things that seeking clearance does not. It furnishes everyone with the reasoning behind what you are about to do and opens a window in which somebody can halt you if the move is hazardous. And it leaves the consequences where they belong: the person who announced retains ownership if it turns out badly, whereas obtaining approval hands the blame to whoever approved. The unassigned coordination work — chasing, welcoming newcomers, prompting, guiding, arranging — is essential to a group succeeding while appearing on no promotion ladder, and it settles on whoever is least able to ignore the problem, which is frequently a newer engineer with a strong sense of duty. The damage is twofold. Those years are the ones in which technical ability is built, and hours spent on organisational chores build none of it, which can hold the career back permanently. Worse, identical work is scored differently by rank: reviewers, hiring panels and managers count it as evidence of leadership from a senior engineer and discount it from a junior one. So absorb it yourself and steer the newer people toward work that advances them. The exercise for producing something removable is to suppose that you personally will have to shut this component down a decade from now, and that your future self will be every bit as busy as you are — which prompts a tidy boundary, a way of seeing who is still calling it, and deliberate separation between systems being joined, with the incidental benefit that what you build is modular and easier to look after.

retired.prompt: An engineer is named technical lead of an eighteen-month effort to replace a logistics scheduling system used by four teams. On day three they are handed a document titled “Goals”, whose first line reads “build a streaming scheduler on a distributed queue”. Two of the four teams have agreed to help; one of them privately expects the project to also retire a reporting tool the lead has never heard of. There is no product manager, and nobody has said who signs off on user-visible behaviour; a director and an engineering manager have each described themselves as “driving” it. The lead's plan is to spend the first month writing the core scheduling engine themselves, since it is the hardest part and they know it best, and to report progress as a percentage of the engine completed. (a) Apply the stated test to the “Goals” document and say what it reveals; name the stage that has been skipped and what it is supposed to produce. (b) The second team's private expectation is a specific named hazard. Name it and say what the lead should do about it. (c) Name the structure missing around leadership, give its four roles with the constraint attached to one of them, and give the two failure patterns it exists to prevent. (d) Assess the first-month plan on two separate grounds — what it does to the lead's availability, and what the proposed progress measure fails to tell anyone.
retired.ideal: (a) The stated test is that if it is difficult to articulate the goals — or if the goals are just a description of your implementation — you have not spent enough time in exploration. “Build a streaming scheduler on a distributed queue” is purely an implementation, so the document fails the test outright. The related rule from design documentation says the same thing from the other side: the goal should not include implementation details, because specifying the technology in the goal means a major design decision has been made without being justified, and the specific implementation should serve the goal, not be the goal. The skipped stage is exploring, which exists to work out the project's true needs and evaluate the approaches available. It should produce: the ability to explain concisely what different teams want in a way they will agree is accurate; a crisp definition of what you are doing, reducible to an elevator pitch; and a clear description of what you are not doing, including how neighbouring projects overlap with or sit inside yours. (b) The hazard is that teams may have agreed to help because they think your project will also achieve some other goal they care about — and they might be wrong. It belongs to the same family as teams holding different mental models of what is being achieved, having unspoken constraints, fixating on niche use cases, or using the same vocabulary to mean different things. The lead should surface it during exploration rather than at delivery: talk to that team and listen to what they actually say and the exact words they use rather than mentally filling in what you wish they had said; get to the point of being able to state their want in a way they agree is accurate; and then state explicitly what the project is not doing, so the mistaken expectation is corrected while correcting it is still cheap. (c) The missing structure is defined roles — at its simplest a table of leadership responsibilities against who owns each, and more formally RACI: Responsible, the person actually doing the work; Accountable, the person ultimately delivering it and signing off that it is done, of whom there is supposed to be only one per task, often the same person as the responsible one; Consulted, people asked for their opinion; and Informed, people kept up to date on progress. The beginning of a project is the best time to lay this out, rather than waiting until two people discover they are doing the same job or work slips through the cracks because nobody thinks it is theirs. The two patterns it exists to break are never making a decision because nobody knows who the decider is, so the group discusses forever, and relitigating every decision over and over because there is no process for making decisions. Its real superpower is that it is an uncontroversial structure, which gives you a way to broach the conversation without it being weird. Note also that with no product manager, someone must own user-visible behaviour and customer requirements — as lead you are implicitly filling any role that does not already have someone in it. (d) Availability. As the person responsible for moving the project along, your time is less predictable than other people's and you will have more meetings than anyone, so if you take on the biggest, most important problems you will take longer to get to the coding work than someone else would — which blocks others and makes you a bottleneck. If you are coding, pick work that is not time-sensitive or on the critical path; better, think of your code as a lever that helps everyone else, pair rather than take over, and avoid becoming a single point of failure. The measure. Percentage of the engine completed reports the lead's own output. The existence of code tells you nothing about whether any problem has actually been solved — in some cases success comes from deleting code — so this cannot show progress toward anything. Success metrics should be agreed with the sponsor and the other leads, and status should be explained in terms of impact: what users can do now and when they will be able to do the next thing.
retired.retired_reason: Part (b) asked the reader to "name" a hazard that the booklet never names — the risk is taught in the Exploring row as an unnamed clause, so the question demanded a term no reader could retrieve. Reissued as p3q1b with (b) rewritten to ask for the risk and the stage at which it must be surfaced.
